utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case on the Appeals Chamber's agenda.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-98-33-A, the Prosecutor versus Radislav Krstic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I would like to make sure that the interpreters are here and that they can hear me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I see the appellant is in the courtroom. Mr. Krstic, can you hear me? THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Defence and Prosecution, I take it that you can hear me. And I would now like, for the record, to ask for the appearances of the parties. Could we first have the appearance for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, President of the Tribunal. Good morning. My name is Nenad Petrusic. With me is Mr. Norman Sepenuk, and today during this hearing and in the appeals proceedings we will have our colleague present, Ms. Sandra Djuric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we now, please, have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. Appearing for the Prosecution is Norman Farrell, Ms. Camille Bibles, Mr. Dan Moylan, and our case manager is Ms. Lourdes Galicia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like now to explain how we are going to proceed during this hearing. As the registrar announced, the case we are hearing today is Prosecutor versus Radislav Krstic. General Krstic was indicted for genocide, complicity to commit genocide, persecution, extermination, murder, and forced transfer or deportation. The indictment concerned the conduct of the accused between July and November 1995, following the attack of the Bosnian Serb forces on the town of Srebrenica. At the time of the attack, General Krstic was the deputy commander and soon thereafter the commander of the Drina Corps, which was, as you know, one of the constituent units of the army of Republika Srpska. The judgement in this case was issued by Trial Chamber I on the 2nd of August, 2001. The Trial Chamber convicted Mr. Krstic of genocide under Article 4 of the Tribunal's Statute; persecution for murders, cruel and inhumane treatment, terrorising the civilian population, forcible transfer and destruction of personal property of Bosnian Muslim civilians, all offences under Article 5; and murder as a violence of the laws and customs of war under Article 3. Both Mr. Krstic and the Prosecution appealed against the judgement. I will say more about the convictions entered by the Trial Chamber against Mr. Krstic and the grounds of both appeals when we reconvene on Wednesday to hear the arguments on the merits. The purpose of today's proceedings, as the parties are aware, is, first, to hear the testimony of the witnesses whose evidence has been admitted on appeal, either as additional evidence pursuant to Rule 115 or as rebuttal material to that evidence. The parties, if they so wish, will be given the opportunity to cross-examine the witnesses. We will also hear the testimony of a witness who has been summoned by the Appeals Chamber proprio motu under Rule 98. Finally, we will hear the arguments of counsel for both the Prosecution and the Defence regarding the weight and the credibility of the admitted evidence and of the admitted rebuttal material. Let me now summarise the evidence which has been admitted in this appeal, and then I will outline in more detail the order in which we will proceed with the testimonies of the witnesses and the arguments of the counsel. First, in its decision of 5 August 2003, the Appeals Chamber admitted into evidence under Rule 115 three documents and a witness statement presented by the Defence. The three documents were tabs 1 through 3 of the Defence Rule 115 motion filed on 10 January 2003. The witness statement was tab 5 of the same motion. I would like to remind the parties that the witness whose evidence was admitted is a protected witness; therefore, he will not be referred to by name. Rather, his statement shall be referred to as "tab 5 evidence." Next, in a decision of 19 November 2003, this past Wednesday, the Appeals Chamber admitted nine documents presented by the Prosecution. These documents were admitted as rebuttal material to the Defence evidence I just described. These nine documents constitute Annexes 1 through 7 and also 11 and 14 of the Prosecution's Notice and Filing of Rebuttal Evidence of 3 October. In this same decision, the Appeals Chamber also ruled admissible as rebuttal material for the Prosecution the evidence given by two witnesses, Mr. Momir Nikolic and Mr. Dragan Obrenovic, in the trial of Prosecutor versus Blagojevic. These witnesses will give their evidence during today's hearing. Also in that decision, the Appeals Chamber ruled on the Prosecution's argument that the evidence in tab 5, which as I already described is the statement of the Defence witness we admitted on 5 August, remains untested and is potentially not credible. The Defence had earlier informed us that it will not be conducting a direct examination of this witness. Given the Prosecution's argument that the veracity of tab 5 evidence may be questionable, the Chamber decided, pursuant to Rule 98, that the witness shall be present during this hearing to be cross-examined by the Prosecution so that the credibility of his evidence could be tested. The Chamber has been informed, however, that the witness whose statement constitutes tab 5 is currently in hospital, and so he will not be present during today's hearing. Also, on Wednesday, 19th of November, the Appeals Chamber rendered a decision summoning proprio motu witness Miroslav Deronjic, whom the Chamber wishes to question concerning the evidence emanating from the sentencing hearing in the case of Prosecutor against Nikolic, because Mr. Deronjic is called as the Appeals Chamber's witness pursuant to Rule 98, the Chamber will conduct the principal examination of the witness. After the Chamber has questioned the witness, the Defence and the Prosecution will be provided with an opportunity to pose questions to the witness. Finally, in a decision rendered yesterday, the 20th of November, the Appeals Chamber granted a motion filed by the Defence and admitted a different portion of the evidence given by Mr. Obrenovic during the Blagojevic trial. Mr. Obrenovic will therefore testify concerning this evidence as well. So that is a summary of the evidence with which this hearing is concerned. Let me now outline the precise order in which we will proceed. This is the order given in our scheduling order of yesterday. First, we will hear from witness Miroslav Deronjic. This witness is appearing as the Chamber's witness. The main examination of the witness will therefore be conducted by the Judges. After the Bench -- after the Bench concludes the questioning, I will give the floor to the Prosecution. The Prosecution will have a maximum of 30 minutes to pose questions to the witness. After that, I will give the floor to the Defence. The Defence will likewise have a maximum of 30 minutes to pose questions. I wish to remind counsel for both the Prosecution and the Defence that they are not obliged to use all the time allocated. After the Prosecution and the Defence finish questioning the witness, the Chamber may pose additional questions. Mr. Deronjic's counsel will be present during his testimony. Next we will hear from witness Dragan Obrenovic. Mr. Obrenovic will first appear as the Defence witness. Therefore, the Defence will conduct the direct examination of the witness. Afterwards, the Prosecution, if it wishes, will be able to cross-examine the witness. Of course, the Judges may also pose questions to Mr. Obrenovic. If they wish to do so, they will ask those questions after the direct examination and the cross-examination are over. Mr. Obrenovic will then testify as the Prosecution's witness. The Prosecution will conduct the direct examination and the Defence will then be permitted, if it wishes, to cross-examine. If the Chamber has additional questions, it will pose them to Mr. Obrenovic after the cross-examination. Mr. Obrenovic's counsel will be present during his testimony, both as -- both as the Defence and as the Prosecution witness. The next witness will be Mr. Momir Nikolic. He will be appearing as the witness for the Prosecution, and so the Prosecution will conduct the direct examination. The Defence will then be given the opportunity to cross-examine Mr. Nikolic. The Chamber may likewise pose additional questions, which will be done at the end of the cross-examination. Mr. Nikolic's counsel will be present during his testimony. I would like to remind counsel for both parties that if they wish -- choose to conduct cross-examination, the scope of that examination must be limited to the scope of the evidence the witness gave during his examination-in-chief. As I already explained, the witness whose evidence was admitted as tab 5 will not be appearing today. After we have heard from all three witnesses, the counsel for both parties will be given the opportunity to present arguments as to the weight and credibility of the evidence admitted on appeal under Rule 115, as well as of the admitted rebuttal material. Each side will be allocated 30 minutes of argument time. I would like the parties to be as precise as possible in their arguments. We will have a lunch break possibly at 11.45, and we will reconvene at 1.15. After that, we will have two breaks of 20 or 30 minutes in the afternoon. We will take those breaks as necessary. I believe we will be able to conclude the evidentiary portion of this appeal today. If, however, we need more time, we will reconvene on Monday, 24th of November. I would like now to turn to Witness Deronjic, and I would like now to call Witness Miroslav Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Deronjic. Can you hear me? I take it you can hear me. Could you please read the solemn declaration given to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. You may now be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Could you -- you can hear me, Mr. Deronjic? Could you please tell the Court your full name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: My name is Miroslav Deronjic. I was born on the 6th of June, 1954.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. What was your address before coming to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was residing in Bratunac. The address was Gavrila Principa Street number 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Deronjic. Mr. Deronjic, the Court has asked you here today to testify in the appeal proceedings in the case of the Prosecutor against Radislav Krstic. As it is the Court itself that has requested your attendance, you will first be asked questions by the Judges. As I'm the Presiding Judge, I will begin the questioning. Following the questions of other Judges, you will then be asked questions by the Prosecution and, after that, by the Defence for Mr. Krstic. Specifically, we will be asking you questions so that you can tell us what you know about what happened during the military operations in Srebrenica during July 1995, the role of Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Mladic, and Mr. Krstic. The witness should feel free to provide the Chamber with the proper context for the information in which he - you, Mr. Deronjic - will be questioned. Mr. Deronjic, I understand that you have a lawyer representing you in the courtroom; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Slobodan Cvijetic. I am Defence counsel for the accused Miroslav Deronjic, who will be heard in this case as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Cvijetic, as is the usual practice, you may make interventions concerning your client's rights but not in relation to the factual basis of his testimony. Mr. Deronjic, you, of course, have the right, as you know, to remain silent. If you feel at any time that questions -- that questions asked may require you to give information that may incriminate you, you may -- you do not have to answer those questions. Thank you very much. Before I commence the questioning, Mr. Deronjic, it is my understanding that you have previously testified before this Tribunal in the Nikolic sentencing procedures on the 28th of October, 2003 in open session. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. And you confirm that you gave that testimony under oath and that it represents the truth to the best of your knowledge? Correct, Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. I therefore formally adopt your testimony from those proceedings into the record for the purposes of this appeal. I will now start with the examination, Mr. Deronjic. Mr. Deronjic, what was your position at the beginning of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the beginning of July 1995, I had the position of president of the Municipal Board of the SDS for Bratunac. I was also a member of the Main Board of the SDS for Republika Srpska. Those were my official positions at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you tell the Court how far is Bratunac from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Bratunac is exactly 10 kilometres from Srebrenica. So the centre of the town of Bratunac, from the centre of the town of Srebrenica, the distance is exactly 10 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Could you -- thank you. Could you briefly tell the Court what were your principal responsibilities as chairman of the Executive Committee of the SDS party in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: If you're referring to the total period of my involvement in the 1990s, then this had to do with questions related to the organisation of the party and the organisation of the multi-party elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1990. After that, in 1995, I engaged in customary party activity linked to the results of the elections and the establishment of the municipal authorities in Bratunac municipality. Afterwards, with the outbreak of the war in 1992, from the period of 20-something April until mid-June, I was president of the Crisis Staff in Bratunac municipality. It is common knowledge that the Serbian Democratic Party was not active in 1992, during the term of the first government of Republika Srpska, headed by Mr. Djeric. In the summer of 1992, the party renewed its activities, and I was co-opted as a member of the Main Board because my predecessor, Mr. Zekic, was killed and somebody from the area needed to represent the area in the SDS Main Board. My activities were the customary activities of a party at municipal level, so I covered party issues in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us about the meeting you had with Mr. Karadzic on the 8th or 9th of July, 1995. What was Mr. Karadzic's position at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, do you wish me to put that within the context of my intention to leave on the 9th, or do you just wish me to explain that particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I would like you to tell us what happened -- what transpired in that meeting. But first, as an introduction to that, I would like you to tell us what exactly was the position of Mr. Karadzic, his official role.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: At that point in time, Your Honour, Karadzic was the president of Republika Srpska. That was his position at the time. I'm not quite sure that he was also president of the SDS. I think that it was Mr. Buha who was president of the party at that time, but I'm not 100 per cent sure. So when I came to talk to him at Pale, he was the current president of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Was he also the Supreme Commander of the armed forces of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. Why did you go to meet him on that date? And where did the meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I shall try briefly to describe the motives for me going to Pale on the 9th or the 8th of May. I'm not quite sure which of those dates is correct. For a brief time, at the beginning of military operations around Srebrenica, I spent some time at the forward command post from which the operations around Srebrenica were commanded, and that area is called Pribicevac. I noted that the operation around Srebrenica went beyond routine operations that had taken place earlier on around Srebrenica. I realised that the scope of that operation went beyond any routine activity. I knew most of the participants in that event, and the bulk of the army in the area was constituted by the Bratunac Brigade. I know most of those men, and I realised that it was highly risky for such serious operations to be undertaken with men who, in my opinion, were not sufficiently well trained for such operations. If necessary, I can explain that in greater detail later on. My intention in going to Pale was to caution the president by saying if there were any serious intentions regarding Srebrenica, which was the conclusion I had made, that it would be a good idea to involve in such an operation another well-trained unit, and I had in mind at that point the unit of the Special Police. It is well known that a minister -- that within the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Republika Srpska there was a Special Police Brigade. I knew the command officers of that unit of Special Police, and I knew personally Mr. Ljubisa Borovcanin, who was head in the staff of that special police unit. For a while, Mr. Borovcanin also performed the duty of chief of public security station in Bratunac. So my intention was, firstly, to see what the military intentions were of the activities around Srebrenica; and secondly, to suggest to President Karadzic that a well-trained unit should be brought to the area, one that would be capable of that type of an operation. Those were my reasons. I went alone to Pale on the assumption that I would find President Karadzic there. I expected him to be somewhere in the Presidency building. At that time, operations along the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road were not taking place, so there was no danger or risk of taking the trip. I arrived at Pale sometime in the afternoon; I can't remember exactly at what time. I entered according to the normal procedure when entering the Presidency building. I wanted to announce my presence and to talk to Mr. Karadzic. En route to the entrance of the president's building, I met Mr. Karadzic, accompanied by Mr. Krajisnik - I'm talking about Momcilo Krajisnik - and also in the company of Mr. Jovica Stanisic, of whom I knew that at the time he held the highest position in the State Security service of the Republic of Serbia. We met, and I described in detail to the Prosecution the area to the left of the Presidency building, and President Karadzic and the others - and I mean Krajisnik - they recognised me. I had never seen Mr. Jovica Stanisic before personally, in real life. Of course, I had seen him on the media before, and of course I recognised him. I went up to the three of them, who were coming in my direction. We exchanged greetings, and President Karadzic introduced me to Stanisic in a way that I had the impression that that group had that day discussed the question of Srebrenica. When introducing me, he said, "This is one of our young men from the ground down there." This was an indication for me that one of the topics they had discussed, among others probably, was the question of Srebrenica. The president at that point in time asked me why I had come, after having introduced me and after we exchanged greetings, and I said that if they had other things to do, I could wait, that it was not urgent, and that I would take up very little of their time, I have just some questions for him. And of course, he assumed that the questions had to do with Srebrenica, where military activities were intensively ongoing. He said, "If it is brief, we can do that here," though I had suggested that I wait until they finish their meeting, because I gathered that the meeting or conversation between them was over because they were leaving the Presidency building and casually walking towards the yard behind the Presidency building. So I assumed that the meeting was over. I thought I'd wait until they saw off Mr. Stanisic, but President Karadzic suggested that I ask him whatever I had to ask him right there, on the spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you for a moment before we return to Mr. Karadzic. You said a few seconds ago that -- you mentioned the question whether there were serious intentions regarding Srebrenica. If there were serious intentions, you wanted to explore this in Pale. What do you mean by "serious intentions regarding Srebrenica," Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, I gave an explanation in detail to the Prosecution, to the effect that in that area, the area of Srebrenica, in 1994 and 1995, a series of such operations, military operations, took place, in the sense of putting up barricades to stop the break-through of Muslim forces into our territory, repair of certain positions, improvement and fortification shifts of our defence lines. That, I would say, were the -- the operations around Srebrenica. However, when I went to Pribicevac in 1995, in the month of July, after a while I came to the conclusion that this operation in Srebrenica was going beyond routine activity and indicates a serious tendency to enter Srebrenica on our part. That's what I meant, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you -- could we return to your meeting with Mr. Karadzic, and could you tell us, please, Witness, what did Mr. Karadzic say regarding his intentions for Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: We stepped aside for a moment, a few steps away from Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Jovica Stanisic, we stood a little to the side, and we started talking about the current events around Srebrenica. I cannot, of course, remember the exact words used in that introductory part. It was the usual exchange of information. I must have told him that I had just come straight from the ground and that I was interested in what was going to happen around Srebrenica, and I remember telling him at one point, "Mr. President, what are your military intentions for the area around Srebrenica?" And at that moment, President Karadzic explained to me that the plan regarding Srebrenica and the purpose of those military operations could be described briefly as two options: The first option, as he told me - and I cannot quote him precisely - but he said something to this effect, "Military operations were to be used to change the actual situation on the ground regarding the UN safe area, as agreed by the act of proclamation of that area." And, you know, Your Honour, that there existed maps that defined this territory marked as the UN safe area under the act of its proclamation. We - and when I say "we" I mean the narrow and broader circle of the Bosnian Serb leadership - expressed our dissatisfaction with the actual situation on the ground, which did not coincide with the exact borders of that area as envisaged by the act of its proclamation as UN safe area. So I understood that Plan A implies that by virtue of military operations, these actual situation on the ground would be made to correspond to what was envisaged by the act of proclamation of the UN safe area, especially because a particular problem for the Serb side was the southern part of this area. In this part, there was a communication line between Skelani and Milici municipalities, and the only road, which was that road, enabled the movement of the army. However, it was controlled all the time by the forces of Bosnian Muslims. I understood that our priority in that Plan A was to free that road and put it in the hands of Bosnian Serbs, thus enabling communication and transportation in that area in the southern part. The Option B, as described to me by President Karadzic, was a conditional plan. In which way conditional? As I understood, it was supposed to enable the entry of the army in Srebrenica if possible. When I say "the possibility," I mean possibility for the Bosnian Serb army. That was the gist of our conversation, and I was happy to hear that in the sense that I was able to understand what the intentions of our army were regarding Srebrenica. On that occasion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, could you tell us, what did Mr. Karadzic -- did Mr. Karadzic refer in this conversation to the Western Slavonia principle? And if so, what did he mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, I thought I would just explain this conversation as it went, but I will answer your question. As we continued talking, Mr. Karadzic asked me -- he said exactly, "What do you think should be done with the population, with the Muslims who were living in Srebrenica?" And he probably meant also both the troops and the civilians. I was surprised by the question at the time, but I answered to the president that I could not possibly imagine the outcome, the epilogue of an entry of our army into Srebrenica. And I said I was not prepared to speculate, because I did not even have the basic indicators that would enable me to make an informed guess. At that moment, I was not even aware whether our army would really go in. I knew it had the intention of going in, if possible, but I didn't know for sure. And I said to the president that at that moment I was not prepared to speculate because I didn't know what course the events would take. And the president then told me something that I remembered; he uttered the sentence that included the words "the principle of Western Slavonia," meaning a possible conduct in the case of entry into Srebrenica. I tried to explain to the president that we - and when I say "we" I mean the leadership of Bosnian Serbs in the broader and the narrower sense - had occasion many times to observe the events that took place in Croatia, the well-known events, and I think it was the 1st of May when the army attacked an area populated by Croatian Serbs, and that area is called Western Slavonia. During that attack, in the unanimous opinion of the then-Serbian leadership, columns of civilians were shelled as they were leaving -- fleeing that area from the attack of Croatian forces. So I understood that sentence to be alluding to those well-known events and the possibility of a repetition of the same course of events as they took place in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Did you understand this to be relevant both with regard to combatants and civilians in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I used these words then: I asked Mr. Karadzic, because I understood his allusion to the recent events in Croatia, and I asked him, "Does that include civilians too?" And he agreed with me that we cannot plan everything that would happen, we cannot speculate, and he said, "We will see, and if we have an opportunity, we will hear from each other." These were not his exact words, but that was the gist of what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: What do you think he meant when he said in that conversation to you - and I quote - "Those people there must be killed"? These were Mr. Karadzic's words.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. At one point he uttered the words, "You need to kill them. You need to kill everyone you can." Those were his words. Your Honour, to be quite honest, at that time I did not give much thought to the sense of those words, because I had no command position that would enable me to engage in such acts, but still I kept thinking about those words. In a sense, since those words were in the context of that reference to Western Slavonia, in my understanding, that meant that fleeing people, including civilians, would be columns that need to be attacked. As I understood, from Western Slavonia the army and civilians fled together, and those columns, those fleeing columns, were attacked by artillery. I do not know the details of those events in Western Slavonia, but that was the essence. So my conclusion was that those columns of fleeing people would be attacked by all available weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: and killed.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course that seems to be the logical conclusion. That's the word he used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Deronjic. After that meeting, the meeting in Pale which we have discussed, you were appointed to a new position. What was that position?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: On the 11th of July, Your Excellency, I was appointed civilian commissioner for the Srebrenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: And could you tell us something about the role or function of that new position as Serb commissioner for Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I will try to explain what functions this position entailed. That night, I asked the president, when I spoke to him on the phone - because I had no prior knowledge that I would be directly involved in any way in the events around Srebrenica - so I asked him on the phone on the 11th, at night, to explain to me the purpose of that position to which I was appointed by an enactment of the presidency of Republika Srpska. And he told me that my primary task was to deal with civilians in the Srebrenica area, because he knew -- he had information to the effect that a great number of civilians had gathered in the area of Potocari around the UNPROFOR base, that is, the base of the Dutch Battalion, which was located within the UN safe area. My other tasks, as he explained --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: My other tasks, as he explained in that telephone conversation on the 11th in the evening, included the following: As soon as conditions were ripe, after the evacuation of the Muslims, were to go into Srebrenica to establish the first government structures, with the primary task of protecting all types of properties, state, social, and all other property, and to make sure that Serbs may return to this area, Serbs who had been dislocated, and of course, to try to repair and restore the infrastructure in and around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. So your conversation, your telephone conversation with Mr. Karadzic about your new appointment as Serb commissioner for Srebrenica, took place on the 11th of July. And I thank you for this information. And could you tell me, please, tell the Court, when did you speak to Mr. Karadzic again, after the 11th?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, do you want me to include telephone conversations as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Exactly. I do.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: In the period that followed, I spoke to Mr. Karadzic, President Karadzic, several times. I remember one conversation that took place on the 12th, for instance, when after the well-known meeting in the Fontana Hotel, I informed President Karadzic of the events that took place at that meeting. I spoke to him from the office of the SDS party in Bratunac. Another conversation of which I have a clear memory had to do with developments regarding the captured Muslims and related to the 13th of July. It could have taken place in the evening hours, I suppose, sometime around 11.00 p.m. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Excuse me. Are you referring to the captured Muslims in Bratunac in this context, Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I meant the Muslims who were captured in Bratunac. They were the focus of that conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: So I had this conversation with President Karadzic from the command post of the Bratunac Brigade. Since it was a very sensitive topic and called for a more discreet way of communication, I decided to use military communications from the command post of the Bratunac Brigade, and I managed to get President Karadzic on the phone and I intended to inform him that on the 13th July at noon, and again in the evening, a large number of Muslim prisoners had arrived and some of them had been detained in various facilities in Bratunac, including school buildings, stadiums, and some were kept inside buses in the centre of the town. And when I speak of Bratunac, I wish you to bear in mind that it is a very small place that has only three streets. It's a very small town indeed. That had created a very bad atmosphere in town. The very presence of a couple of thousand captured Muslims represented a big problem for that small town, because most men of military age were already engaged on the front line and the risk of escape of those captives was high, because they -- the security was very poor in the facilities where they were kept. Certain murders had already taken place. I had information as of the 13th in the evening that certain -- that some murders had taken place in the school building, and it was my intention to inform President Karadzic of all these things, so I went to talk to him from the command post on the 13th in the evening. And if you want me to, I can describe that conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I contacted President Karadzic, and most of our communication was indirect. I explained already to the Prosecution that I don't know exactly how this communication uses relays, but I know that there were mediators who occasionally butted into our conversation. I would hear a voice that says, "You can now speak to President Karadzic," and then I would hear his instructions. That conversation did not last long. I expressed my concern over the situation in Bratunac and suggested to him that there were already murders taking place. I cannot remember every sentence I said, but I said that in view of the presence of international forces and representatives of the press it was madness to allow such things to happen in the town of Bratunac and the very detention of people in inadequate places was a problem in itself that was obvious to anyone who had any interest in it. President Karadzic told me briefly that a man would come - that's exactly what he said - a man would come who would be carrying instructions as to how to deal with these prisoners, and he uttered one sentence which I remembered verbatim, and I must say that I conveyed this information precisely even before I saw the text of that conversation given to me by the Prosecution. That sentence was: "The goods must be in storehouses -- in warehouses by dawn and not there but elsewhere." That was the sentence uttered by President Karadzic. He was trying to tell me in code the gist of the instructions that would be brought by that man who was supposed to come to Bratunac. And then when he finally asked me if I had understood, I told him that I did; although, I wasn't quite sure I had well understood what he meant by "elsewhere," although I had my ideas. So after that conversation, I went back to my office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: How did you understand those words "the goods must be in storehouses -- in warehouses by dawn and not there but elsewhere"? What at the time was your understanding, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, my understanding of that message I have explained, and that is what I told the gentleman who later appeared carrying instructions. Thinking about what these words "elsewhere" meant, I gathered the president wanted those men to leave Bratunac in the first place; that was quite clear; that nothing should be done with the prisoners in Bratunac, nothing at all. And this word "elsewhere" meant, according to what I inferred - the president didn't say so - the only logical place to put up so many people close to Bratunac was Bijeljina, and there was a large prison there in the environs of Bijeljina. It was a military prison which had a capacity, according to information I had - I was never there - I heard it was a large prison and that there was adequate space for putting up those people in the prison there. This interpretation of Mr. Karadzic's sentence was what I conveyed to Mr. Beara, who appeared in my office in the evening of the 13th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So was Mr. -- or Colonel Beara the emissary or the person from President Karadzic? And if so, what exactly did Mr. Beara tell you when he came to see you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Beara was, in my opinion, an emissary of Mr. Karadzic's because no one else on that day, the 13th or the 14th, appeared with any kind of instructions regarding the treatment of the imprisoned Muslims, so that is the conclusion I reached, though I cannot claim that it is absolutely correct. When Mr. Beara came to my office, never for a moment did he say that he was coming directly from Karadzic. The only thing he did say was that his orders were from the top, from above, from the top. I'm not sure whether he said "from above" or "from the top," but basically both mean the same. So I inferred that he was coming following orders and instructions from Mr. Karadzic. I had information that during the night a part of the prisoners from Bratunac were being taken via Konjevic Polje to Zvornik; anyway, in that direction, because that is the same direction Zvornik to Bijeljina. So at that point in time, I didn't know exactly whether they were being driven to Zvornik or Bijeljina. So my logical conclusion was that he had come to continue this process of taking the Muslim prisoners from Bratunac in the direction of Konjevic Polje and Bijeljina. However, during this encounter I described the details - I think there's no need for me to repeat it - but -- regarding the atmosphere in my office, because I have to tell you, Your Honours, that I did not expect this gentleman, Beara, to come necessarily to see me in my office, because President Karadzic didn't say that he would come to see me. He just said a man would come with instructions. But this possibility was not excluded so I did assume that he might come to see me as well, and he did. This was late in the evening. I cannot say exactly what time it was, but I think it was after midnight. He was in a rather inebriated condition, under the influence of alcohol. This was quite visible at first glance. But not to such an extent that he had no control of his behaviour, but he had obviously consumed quite a bit of alcohol. And this is confirmed by other witnesses. His behaviour in my office was a big surprise for me, because after a few introductory remarks, congratulations, ceremonial greetings, he insisted on a drink. So I went out and found some alcohol, we had a drink. And then he said hat he was coming -- or actually, he started by saying, "I have come in connection with these prisoners. All of them should be killed here in Bratunac." I was surprised by the way in which he said that. And, on the other hand, this was in contradiction with the instructions, or at least my interpretation of the instructions, I had received from President Karadzic by telephone. I then decided to ask Mr. Simic, Ljubisav Simic, who was president of the municipality in Bratunac, to go home, as he looked rather tired and he needed sleep, and he was also a bit tipsy, and he agreed. I took him out of the office and asked him to go home. I told him that the next morning I was going to Pale, I had a scheduled meeting with Karadzic, and that he should come to the office early in the morning because there were many important things to do, that he should be there. So I went back to the office and I said to Mr. Beara the exact instructions I had received from President Karadzic, and I told him that no killings or any kind of acts in relation to the prisoners could be done in Bratunac and that the instructions I had from the president were that those people should be taken to Batkovic. This word "Batkovic," I repeat, was my own conclusion. It was not mentioned in the instructions I was given by the president, but my conclusion was that that was the only place where those captured prisoners could be put up. After these comments of mine, Mr. Beara, in a rather surprised tone, asked me or said to me, "Mr. Deronjic" - or president or whatever it was he called me - "I have instructions from above" - that is what he said then, from the top - "that those people should be killed in Bratunac." I continued to insist and said that I would go to Pale in the morning and that I had no such instructions, that I wouldn't allow any such things, including killings that he mentioned, to take place in Bratunac. The conversation ended after we exchanged a few more sentences about this, and at one point I realised that he sort of said, "All right. That is how I will act, or I'll check that." I had the impression that I had convinced him, that I had persuaded him that no killings or any such things could be done in Bratunac. He left my office, and I went home with the intention of going early in the morning to Pale to talk to the president. That would be briefly or maybe in some detail my description of my conversation with President Karadzic on the 13th of July and my conversation with the man who came with these instructions on the 13th or the 14th early in the morning of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. So on the 14th of July, you went to Pale to see the president. Did this meeting take place? And what happened there, if it did?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In the morning of the 14th of July, after staying in Bratunac briefly - I think it is important for me to tell you about this - one of the men informed me early in the morning that Mr. Beara had gone to a company in Bratunac called Ciglana, which manufactured bricks, and that he wanted to do something there with the detained Muslims. In view of the conversation we had had the previous night, I came to the conclusion that he wanted to kill some people or liquidate them there in Bratunac. I got in my car and headed towards that factory, and I met Mr. Beara at -- on a small bridge on the way out of Bratunac. It is a road going towards Ljubovija and Serbia. We quarrelled there again briefly but fervently. I repeated that I was on my way to Pale to see President Karadzic and that I insisted that nothing should be done, including killings, in Bratunac. He very angrily said, "I wanted to see whether they could be locked up there." There was a warehouse over there, and this, I think, was a possibility. But I feared the worst. I feared that those men might be killed in Bratunac, and I said again that no locking up or anything else could be considered in Bratunac. He angrily got in the car and said, "Okay," and we parted there on the bridge. I waited for a brief time in Bratunac, and I saw that the whole thing was over, in the sense that the buses were leaving towards Zvornik. I went to Pale that day, I met with President Karadzic at his invitation, in his office, and we spoke on the 14th of July. I will tell you with precision what it was we spoke about. The first topic we discussed was the question of the evacuation of civilians from Potocari. I informed him in detail about the course of the negotiations at the Fontana Hotel, which I had attended. I explained the evacuation, including all the details that might have been of interest for the president at the time, and my assumptions also, that about 20.000 civilians had been transported from Potocari during the 12th and the 13th of July, as on the 13th of July I think the transportation of civilians from Potocari was over. I explained the way in which this transportation was carried out, and I told him that from the first transports, that is, those that took place on the 12th of July - or at least, that was the information I had - the men had been separated from those convoys and detained. I didn't know the exact number. I don't even know the number today. It wasn't such a large number, but I do know that they were held in the prison in Bratunac, in the Public Security Station in Bratunac, and also in the prison at the command, in the headquarters. And I passed on this information to President Karadzic. As for the transportation of civilians, that was roughly what we discussed. I can't remember any other details. Perhaps we commented on the behaviour of the UNPROFOR forces and things like that. After that, we tackled the topic of the fate of the detainees. A second very important topic was for me to brief him as to what had happened to the captured Muslims in Bratunac. I quoted literally the sentence that I was given by Mr. Beara as being his instructions. I said, "Mr. President, Beara came to my office." I described briefly the atmosphere in the office at the time, the customary business, and I said that Mr. Beara literally told me the following: "I have instructions from the top that these men should be killed in Bratunac." I stopped there and waited for the president's reaction to this. The president said, "Those soldiers are either fools or madmen," or something to that effect. I'm not sure about the exact words, but the meaning of what he said was that those soldiers were not normal, or something along those lines. We continued the conversation, and I told him that I had persuaded Mr. Beara and that the convoys were already leaving in the direction of Zvornik and that those men were being taken in that direction. I also told him that I had information that on the 13th already some convoys were going towards Zvornik. Some buses had already gone there. We also discussed these matters, and the meeting was quite a lengthy one, but I think that the -- I have conveyed the gist of that conversation. If you are interested in any particular details, I'll be glad to convey them to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you tell me a little bit more about the reaction of the -- of President Karadzic to what you reported to him about your conversation with Colonel Beara. In other words, did he say anything more about those killings or executions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Of course I informed the president, and I omitted to mention that, about the incidents in connection with the detained or captured Muslims that I was aware of up until that time, that is, the 14th in the morning. A major incident or a major tragedy that occurred on the 13th in the evening was the killing of a large number of Muslims in the agricultural cooperative farm in Kravica. Muslims were held there, and I received this information from the ground -- or the Muslims who had surrendered. When I say "captured" I include those who voluntarily surrendered. And an incident broke out between the army of Republika Srpska, members of the police, the special police forces, and those captured Muslims. A killing occurred of several Serb policemen - one, actually - and several were wounded in this clash. And then the policemen or soldiers, whoever was there - I don't know with precision - took their revenge on those captured men, and according to information passed on to me by Mr. Borovcanin, about 300 men were killed. I really do not wish to speculate about these numbers, I am just saying that this was the information conveyed to me by Mr. Borovcanin. I passed on this same information to Mr. Karadzic, considering it to be a major incident and event that he should be informed of. He uttered a few sentences, saying that our forces had been provoked by the attack against them and the killing of this policeman at the checkpoint. I said that this could be considered retaliation, but of course it was a terrible kind of revenge, because a large number of people were killed because of that incident. We didn't comment at length about that event, but he asked me whether I knew what had been done with the bodies of the men killed. I couldn't tell him anything about that, because I had not asked, when I was told about it, what had been done with the bodies. I told him that I had information that during the 13th there had been killings of smaller proportions, as I had been told, in the area of Konjevic Polje, that small groups of captives or Muslim soldiers had been killed in the area. I told him that I had passed along that route - of course, he knew that because that was the only route I could have taken - and that I had seen groups of detained Muslims along the length of that route and a large group in Kasaba, a village towards Milici; in the stadium a large group; and several smaller groups along the road that were secured by the police and the army. I passed on all these reports to President Karadzic. He did not comment at any length on these events. What I have remembered as his reaction I have told you about. I assume that he must have said a few more sentences, but I haven't memorised them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Deronjic. Finally, I would like to ask you about a meeting which you have mentioned which took place at the Hotel Fontana a few days earlier, I believe, on the 12th of July at 10.00 a.m. Is that correct? There was such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is correct. This meeting did take place, and what I said a moment ago was precisely related to that meeting that took place in the Fontana Hotel on the 12th of July at noon, in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mladic and Krstic were present at that meeting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I must say that in my first interview I failed to mention Mr. Krstic because I had not noticed him. Later, from the recordings that I saw, since there is a wealth of recordings of that meeting, I saw that Mr. Krstic had been at that meeting. I know today that he was at that meeting, and of course Mr. Mladic was there and he even chaired the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Do you remember what was discussed at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour, I remember clearly the gist of those discussions. I cannot quote exact words, but it was a conversation, it was a discussion between the representatives of the Muslims who had come to that meeting to present the position of Muslim civilians who were at that time located in Potocari; the commanding officers of the Dutch forces, who were there in the capacity of witnesses or perhaps security for the Muslim representatives; and the command of the military forces of Republika Srpska; and there were several of us civilians from the Bratunac municipality, including president of the municipality, Mr. Simic; president of the Executive Board, Mr. Davidovic; and myself. At that time, I had already taken up my position of civilian commissioner for the area of Srebrenica. The course of that meeting was very interesting, curious in the sense that it was some kind, as I later concluded, of smoke screen for the public, because it was recorded by TV cameras to leave the impression -- to create the impression of a regular meeting, on which Mladic insisted very much, and it later turned out that the meeting was not so important after all, because most of the contacts with Muslims and most decisions had been made outside that meeting that was held at noon on the 12th in the Fontana Hotel. I was questioned about this event, and I conveyed the gist of the discussions at that meeting, where, among other things, Mladic offered to the Muslim side that everybody who surrenders until the end of that day or some particular hour on that day - I'm not sure any more - would be allowed to leave the Srebrenica safe area. And Muslim representatives also said a few words, presenting their position; whereas, I also availed myself of the opportunity to explain what were my instructions from President Karadzic regarding the treatment of civilians in Potocari. And if you allow me, Your Honour, I would like to tell you now what instructions I had regarding the treatment of those civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: On the 11th, in the evening, when I spoke to President Karadzic on the phone, which conversation I've already described, I received instructions in the form of three options that I was supposed to offer to the Muslim side regarding their fate and the future. The first option assumed that they would remain in that area, in fact that civilians could go back to their homes; and the second option was for them to leave for the territory controlled by their forces, using the shortest route, I suppose; and the third option was rather odd, and I exchanged a few words about it with the president, because it involved third countries, as President Karadzic told me. I asked him, "What do you mean by 'third countries', Mr. President?" And he said, "Well, I don't know exactly. Maybe there are some third countries or there will be some third countries who would be prepared to receive these people, these refugees." He told me to convey these three options at that meeting, and I did so. I did so briefly, and I wanted to add a few things. I quoted one instruction from the president; namely, that if among those civilians our intelligence officers, both military and civilian, recognise anybody who they know to be guilty of crimes against our civilians, they would be kept prisoner. Mladic interrupted me, however, at that meeting, although I was going to go on, but he decided otherwise and interrupted the meeting at that point. Although, before that happened, the Muslims had expressed their concern and fear and their desire to leave that area as soon as possible, insisting, of course, on security and escort being provided by the international forces present in that area; namely, the Dutch Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Had you had any contacts that day -- additional contacts with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Not on that day or in the following days did I see Mr. Mladic. I don't believe I ever saw him again until I was arrested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: On the 12th or thereabout, did you have any contacts with General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, there were no contacts either at the meeting or afterwards between me and Mr. Krstic. I don't remember seeing him after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So during that meeting, the role of General Krstic was basically -- he was quiet? Did he say anything? Can you try to remember. I'm speaking of the Fontana meeting.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, not that I noticed. And I am certain that Mr. Krstic did not utter a word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This completes my questioning of the witness. And I thank you for your answers. And I will now ask my fellow Judges if they would ask you -- want to ask you further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Just a second. Let's first look at the timetable. We can still continue. There's no problem. So who goes first? May I ask my colleague Judge Shahabuddeen to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, I would ask you one question about how you understood Mr. Karadzic's statement that the soldiers were fools or something to that effect. How did you understand him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, at that moment when Mr. Karadzic told me that, there were only two possible conclusions. I, of course, made no comments on what the president said to my report, but there are only two ways of understanding this: One is that he meant that the soldiers were crazy to be doing something that he hadn't ordered; that is one possible logical conclusion. Another one is that he meant that Mr. Beara was completely indiscreet and acted completely inappropriately under the circumstances in uttering those instructions. However, I have to admit that I did not give it much thought then or analysed his words. However, I did think about it later, and today, when you ask me this question, I must say that this first conclusion should be rejected because on the 14th the president knew about the intentions of the army, and even if he had not given them such instructions, he was in a position to prevent them. And as I told the Prosecution already, I believe his comment referred to the indiscretion that Mr. Beara displayed in giving these instructions at my office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: One other question or a set of questions: You held a position of importance. The President has referred to the Hotel Fontana meeting at which you were present. Now, I think you said that you conveyed the gist of your conversation with President Karadzic. Did you regard it as important that the top levels of the army should be functioning in harmony with the opinions held by President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, I was absolutely convinced that that was important and that troops were under obligation to act on the instructions of the president, who was at that time also Supreme Commander of the army of Republika Srpska. And I omitted to say earlier that just before that meeting on the 12th, I was invited by General Mladic to the Fontana Hotel and we had a very unpleasant conversation discussing the same topic that you mentioned. He used very vulgar words to describe the president and my own position. And I understood what his position was, and I tried to describe that atmosphere, that very bad atmosphere, in my interviews with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: When you said that you conveyed the gist of your conversations with President Karadzic, would I be right in the impression that the gist of the conversations would have included President Karadzic's reference to the Slavonia principle?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The instructions I received related at that time exclusively to the civilian population that was located in Potocari. President Karadzic told me on the 11th that he had information that a large number of civilian population from Srebrenica were in Potocari. Instructions regarding the treatment of those people, which included a large number of women and children, related to those three options that I described, and that applied only to the civilians in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So in your understanding, President Karadzic's reference to the Slavonia principle referred to what group of people?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, I will try to explain what I meant. It is, of course, very complicated, because neither the president nor I, at the time when he gave those instructions, alluding clearly to the events in Croatia, knew precisely what could happen in Srebrenica. I suppose that President Karadzic meant that one of the possible denouements was that both the troops and the civilians would flee in the same direction and those fleeing columns should be attacked, shelled. And the army, the soldiers, really ran for Tuzla, in the intention of making a break-through there; whereas, a large group of civilians went another way and remained in the safe area of the UNPROFOR base. And I suppose that when the president told me about the principle of conduct and the options I mentioned, meant only the civilians in Potocari because no one had been captured or had surrendered at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] One last question: President Karadzic, in his conversation with you, spoke of killing people. Did you mention that at all at the Hotel Fontana meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No. I absolutely did not mention the possibility of killing, nor had I conveyed President Karadzic's instruction to anyone before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You did not regard that element as having any importance.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: It cannot be qualified that way, that I did not consider it important, but I thought that the president was not telling me in order to convey it to somebody else but just so as to inform me of the possible outcome. And in his orders that he gave as Supreme Commander, he issued exact, precise instructions that would cater to all the possible epilogues of the action. I did not think it necessary or fitting to convey such information to anyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Witness, before giving the floor over to my other distinguished colleagues, I'd like to return for a moment to your last answer to my distinguished colleague Judge Shahabuddeen. I have -- I had the impression from your description of the Fontana Hotel meeting that the reason why there was no more specific reference to the killings or executions, because the meeting was intended as a smoke screen because Muslim representatives were present there. Was my understanding correct of that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Precisely that is the kind of conclusion I meant, and I think your conclusion is quite correct. I just have to add one more sentence: The presence of international forces, that is the UNPROFOR command, at the meeting and the presence of the press could also be a reason for such behaviour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I would like to move on now to Judge Pocar, vice-president, who expressed interest in asking questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, President, but in light of the last questions that have been put to the witness, I don't have any additional question to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you very much. Judge Guney. Judge Guney, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have already indicated that during your meeting with General Mladic at the Fontana Hotel you had an exchange of views and you said that he was vulgar in his behaviour. Could you please elaborate a little on that point.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, I was speaking of a meeting prior to this official meeting at 10.00. We met upon the invitation of Mr. Mladic in the Fontana in the morning prior to that meeting. I cannot tell you exactly at what time, though I did say that I thought it could have been between 7.00 and 8.00 in the morning. So this was in preparation of this other meeting. And Mr. Mladic told me to come to the Fontana for us probably to agree on the course of the meeting that had been scheduled for that day at 10.00. As far as I can remember, there was breakfast being served, and during that breakfast I found Mr. Simic, the president of the municipality, there; as far as I can remember, also Mr. Vasic, head of the public security; and several others. I introduced myself because I was never sure to what extent Mladic knew me at all. I think he didn't really distinguish me from others, because we didn't have much occasion to meet. I told him what my position was, and his comments were rather vulgar in response to that. He asked me something to the effect - of course, I can't quote his words because this was eight years ago - he said, "Gentlemen, you're walking around here in civilian clothes," because there was no combat, there was no need for me to wear a uniform on that day. Then he also said words to the effect that "Where is, President Karadzic? Why didn't he enter Srebrenica with me? Here I am capturing Srebrenica, and you civilians, just like that." Those were the kind of comments he made, which I thought were quite unacceptable. I continued the conversation with Mr. Mladic. I was rather nervous. I said that I didn't want to polemicise with him about those matters but that I had instructions from the president which I wanted to present at the meeting. And then he spoke very -- in very crude terms. He cursed the president, and he said, "Why didn't he come to enter Srebrenica," to that effect. And I left that meeting very shortly afterwards. I returned to my office, and I said I would come back at 10.00. And I tried, without having any permission from Mr. Mladic, who chaired that meeting, to refer to the instructions I had been given by President Karadzic. He cut me short very roughly. He said, "Sit down. What have you got to talk about?" And that is how that meeting ended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I thank my distinguished colleague Judge Guney. We will now -- in a moment, we will break until 1.15. And I would like just to say a word about how we will continue thereafter. First, there will be some questions from my distinguished colleague Judge Schomburg. And after that, the witness, Mr. Deronjic, will be examined first by the Prosecution and then by the Defence. So we will now rise, and we will resume at 1.15. Thank you. --- Luncheon recess taken at 11.49 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. We will now resume questioning of Mr. Miroslav Deronjic, our witness today, and we are still at the stage of questions from the Bench. I will now call on my distinguished colleague Judge Schomburg to ask his questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Deronjic, can you please tell the Court, when did you become actually president of the Crisis Staff in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, Your Honours, I became president of the Crisis Staff of Bratunac municipality towards the end of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When did you meet for the first time Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, I don't recollect the first meeting. The first time I saw Karadzic was at a rally in Vlasenica in 1990, when there was a promotional rally for the SDS. But on that occasion, I had no personal contact with President Karadzic. In the period after that - and I'm talking about 1990 - I did have some personal contacts with President Karadzic linked to events that are well known, but mainly in connection with the preparations that were held in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1990 and the subsequent implementation of the election results.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you yourself participate in a meeting on the 14th and 15th October 1991 of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: On the 14th of October, in 1991, if that was the Assembly meeting -- allow me a little time to try and remember. I did attend another Assembly meeting, I think it was in December 1991, whereas, on the 14th and 15th of October, I do not think I took part. But allow me to add that in my capacity as president of the Municipal Board, I did attend a meeting linked to the events that were reviewed at that Assembly, but during the war nor in any period was I ever a deputy in the Assembly, a member of parliament.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you -- you made reference to December 1991. Is it the meeting of the 19th of December presided over by Radovan Karadzic you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the very meeting I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please in context describe us the development and the kind of relationship between you and Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, I shall try to be very brief and explain. You put it very well when you said "the development of the relationship" between President Karadzic and myself. I think that is the real expression because those relationship -- that relationship changed and developed from 1990, when they were within the normal relationships you would expect between the president of the party and the president of a small local board. However, in 1990, they changed significantly, and I'll explain why. It is a well-known fact that in 1993, I was elected or, rather, co-opted to the Main Board, when the party renewed its activities, having been frozen for a year, and in the place of the late Goran Zekic, who used to represent the area in the Main Board before. I had been a member of the personnel commission of the SDS earlier on, and I don't remember any meeting from the earlier period, because I was elected at the end of 1991 and shortly after that, the war prevented my active participation in the work of that commission. Of course, in 1993, when the party renewed its work, I did have occasion as a member of the Main Board to meet the state and political leadership of Republika Srpska, and I would frequently, at meetings of the personnel commission, see the president of the party and the president of the republic, Radovan Karadzic, and these meetings involved a smaller number of people, so we were able to review a number of issues, even outside the agenda that was scheduled for such meetings. Up until 1995, that relationship evolved to reach what would I -- what I would describe as a relationship of mutual respect between me and the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you go that far to call it a friendship?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, for my part, I can try and define it. I don't dare to be so bold as to say that I was an intimate friend of President Karadzic, because I hadn't known him before all these events. He had a far larger number of friends and acquaintances from the earlier period who were in the leadership of the party and the state. I could list many of them. But my relationship with President Karadzic in 1995 was certainly more than would be a customary -- a normal relationship between the president of the party and the president of a Municipal Board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Am I correct in assuming that whenever an instruction was given to you by Mr. Karadzic you would follow this instruction already since this meeting in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: If those instructions referred to normal activities, of course I carried them out. I do not remember any activity that I did not implement that had to do with the activities of the party. That is what I'm referring to primarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This brings me to the next question: How would you describe the relationship between the civil leaders, civilian leaders, and the military leaders? Were they on equal footing?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand the interpretation. I beg your pardon. The term used is a bit vague. Equal; I see. I see. I wouldn't be so bold as to say that they were relations of equality, especially at lower levels, between the civilian bodies and the army. There were quite a number of problems that burdened those relations. As for my behaviour during the war, that I have described in detail in my statement for the Prosecution, shows that those relationships were frequently disrupted. I personally did my best not to contribute to any disruption of those relations, but basically the military leadership, both on the ground and at a higher level, would frequently turn a deaf ear to certain demands of the civilian bodies. I couldn't list any details in that connection because I'm not familiar with them, except those that occurred at my local level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is it correct that since 1991 until 1995 - the question in time we're discussing in this case, the time in question - once again the question: You followed the instructions - and I am now referring precisely to those instructions, where explained already in December 1991 to the participants of that meeting attended by you, and these instructions precisely identifying the steps to be taken within the respective municipalities in order to establish Bosnian Serb control. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour, including, as I said - and which is in the factual statements - certain measures that I implemented in the joint Assembly in Bratunac. I did implement all the instructions linked to that, and your conclusion is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So coming back to the question of the general -- of the relationship between civilian leaders and military leaders in general. In your own guilty plea, you admitted that you yourself coordinated and monitored the attack on Glogova in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So am I correct in assuming that military forces would follow your instructions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, there is a fundamental difference in the organisation of the army of Republika Srpska in 1992 and the army which was fully organised in 1995. I should like to mention that the event in Glogova occurred on the 8th of May, when the only legitimate, legal armed force in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and therefore in Bosnia as well, was the Yugoslav People's Army. We had a unit of Territorial Defence in those days which was not linked up into a single whole, nor were those activities of the TO coordinating or regulated properly. There were just these municipal units of Territorial Defence and the army of Republika Srpska, as far as I can recollect - and I think I am right - was organised by a decision of the Presidency of the 15th of May or after that date, after the withdrawal of the army of Yugoslavia from Bosnia and Herzegovina by order of the Supreme Commander of the JNA at the time, Mr. Kostic. It was then that the army of Republika Srpska was organised differently. There were officers, personnel, and organisational units in all the municipalities. Under those conditions, the civilian bodies, the local bodies, did not have any particular assignments, nor was I involved in them. So as of 1992, there was a separation between the functioning of civilian and military bodies on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Maybe we have to come back later to this point. You do not dispute that what you said the 30th of September, 2003 in a hearing in this Tribunal, that you yourself authorised soldiers to bomb the houses of Glogova and they were burned and effectively at least 65 Bosnian Muslims were murdered, and you met in Pale in May 1992, immediately after these events, a number of persons in order to celebrate this, amongst those Mr. Karadzic; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I am not denying any of the facts that you have mentioned. Only I wouldn't say that I ever admitted that on the 10th or 11th or 12th of May, when I went to Pale, that we celebrated the event. I went upon the -- upon an invitation to that meeting to brief the military and civilian leadership of what was going on in Bratunac municipality, and I reported on the events in Glogova, and it is true that I said that because of those events I was applauded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Who else was present in this meeting, besides Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, the meeting was also attended by Mr. Mladic and Mr. Ostojic, who in those days was president of the Executive Board of the SDS of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is it correct when -- that when Serb forces overtook a certain area on the map in Pale this area was designated by the colour blue?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That is true, especially regarding what I saw, that is, the area of Bratunac. So I confirmed that in my statement. But this was a comment made by Mr. Ostojic. I didn't see whether at that particular meeting or maybe later he coloured it in blue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you later see the same map and what was the -- in which colour could you -- if so, in which colour could you see the Srebrenica area in 1995? Was this procedure continued?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I really am unable to recollect, nor did I ever again see the map or Srebrenica or any other area being coloured in any particular colour. I really don't remember that, and I claim that I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Well, when did you meet for the first time Mr. Krstic?
