utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, in my life I saw Mr. Krstic for the first time at the beginning of July at Pribicevac, the advance command post, which is geographically a plateau above Srebrenica. I cannot tell you the exact date, but I think -- no, I'm not sure that it was in the beginning of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So if I understand it correctly, before the 11th, 12th, 13th of July. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct. That was the beginning of July, and certainly before the 11th and the 12th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you please explain to the Court in context what was the content of your discussion or discussions you had between the first meeting and the meetings in Hotel Fontana with Mr. Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I shall try to explain briefly. The area from which there were commands for the military operation of Srebrenica, I left that area at the beginning of July. The reason was very simple: Because everyone was mobilised and I felt awkward being in town at the time, and I said that I didn't have information of the significance of the military operation over Srebrenica. When going to that command post, maybe the first or the second day, when I arrived there, I noticed Mr. Krstic at that position. Mr. Krstic was dealing with military matters, that is, orders linked to the operation itself; that is how I understood his role. In front of the command at that advance command post, there was a table in the open air. I think, though I'm not a hundred per cent sure, that we just greeted one another. Mr. Krstic, I assume, didn't know me. I introduced myself. And I don't remember anything serious we may have discussed. I simply realised that he was busy issuing orders about Srebrenica, so I didn't wish to bother him there at the command post. It's quite possible that we spent five or six minutes together, then I moved away from that position. The second time I saw him - and this is something that I omitted to mention during my first statement - it was at the Fontana Hotel. Today I know for certain that he was there. I didn't have any personal contact or conversation with Mr. Krstic at that time, on that occasion. That is all the time I ever spent with Mr. Krstic. I had never seen him before, though I knew that he was one of the commanders in the Romanija area, but we never had occasion to meet or see one another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Coming back to questions already answered in part by you on the basis of the questions put to you by my distinguished colleagues, would the assessment be correct that the meeting in Hotel Fontana was more or less a farce, taking into account that Muslims were present, the international press was present, and it was absolutely no possibility to give any kind of serious instruction or information to anybody in the room?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, with the addition of a minor correction. The meeting was not attended by representatives of the international press or the media. Present at the meeting was a team of reporters of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, and I knew one of those journalists. The fact that the cameras were turned on and that this gathering was being filmed speaks in favour of my thesis, and also, of course, the presence of representatives of the international forces at the meeting. The behaviour of Mr. Karadzic at the meeting, which was contrary to what happened later on to the people from Srebrenica, speaks in support of my thesis that the meeting was a farce. Let me add to this the knowledge I gained later on, when I realised that Commander Mladic had had previously meetings with representatives of the Muslims and that at those meetings he had threatened the Muslim representatives. I learnt about this when the Prosecution showed me the evidence during my testimony, and this also supports my thesis. At the meeting in Bratunac, he acted quite contrary to the way in which he acted at the meetings that preceded that one and, of course, contrary to the tragic epilogue of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Am I correct in assuming that, as you told us previously, one of the purposes why you attended this meeting was to convey the gist of your discussions with Mr. Karadzic, with whom you had, as we have elaborated now, a relatively good contact at said point in time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is quite correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And in which way did you convey this message from Karadzic to the addressees?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, I was speaking about instructions with regard to treatment of civilians who were at that point in time in Potocari or heading towards it. I received those instructions by telephone, and there are witnesses of this in the command of the Bratunac Brigade. And I conveyed those instructions at the meeting. I didn't have time to convey some of the explanations given by the president, but I think that I did convey what was the gist of it and what was relevant for the meeting. I said that, after that, Mladic interrupted me rather rudely and that is how the meeting ended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This morning you mentioned, transcript page 26, line 18, and page 27, line 20, inter alia, that one of your goals was that killings did not happen in your jurisdiction - put it this way - did not happen in Bratunac. What did you do in order that this goal be realised by the militarily responsible persons?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: My contacts, Your Excellency, at that moment with military authorities were zero, so I had no chance to directly contact any of the competent commanding officers of the army of Republika Srpska who were located on the ground. I had no communication with them. According to the information that I had about incidents and major events, such as, for instance, the event in Luka or the cooperative farm in Kravica, rather, I informed President Karadzic, conveying all the information I had about the events in Bratunac regarding also the crimes of killings of people in the primary school and other places, depending on what I knew at the time. Regarding my ability to contact General Mladic, it was zero. I had absolutely no way of contacting him at that time, because combat was going on, an offensive was taking place, and the armed clashes between Serb forces and Muslim forces who were trying to break through to Tuzla, through Konjevic Polje, were ongoing. I went out to the command post twice in those days, and I did not find anyone on any of those occasions. I only found one lower-ranking officer, and I didn't even know that he was an officer; his name was Milomir Stanojevic. I did not see any other officer in the headquarters at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You have nearly answered my final question, but to put it nevertheless to you: Did you at any point in time after the meeting in Hotel Fontana meet General Krstic or see him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, never again after that meeting - and I mentioned that I didn't even see him during the meeting - did I see Mr. Krstic again. Soon after that meeting, I received information about the movements of the army of Republika Srpska towards the next safe area in that region, that is, Zepa or Gorazde, and from what I heard from other people Mr. Krstic had left the area together with the troops, so I was not even able to see him at that time. He never visited my office, and I never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Only one final clarification, because -- maybe I misunderstood you this morning. Now you said, "I didn't even see him during the meeting"; whereas, to the best of my recollection - but it may be wrong - you told us this morning that you saw no reaction and you didn't hear any word from Mr. Krstic. So how can you come to this conclusion when you even didn't see him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, I see that you have omitted one fact. I know that Mr. Krstic was at that meeting, and I remember clearly who spoke at the meeting. I would have noticed and I would have remembered if Krstic had spoken. Since he did not take the floor - and the two things are not mutually exclusive - I did not notice him at the time and he did not speak. If you need any further clarification, I'm at your disposal. But I know very well who spoke at that meeting. I did not notice him at the time, and I certainly would have remembered if he had spoken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Schomburg. I now call on the vice-president, Judge Pocar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to put a couple of additional questions to Mr. Deronjic. First, referring to the last question that has just been put by Judge Schomburg, am I correct in understanding that on the 12th of July at the Hotel Fontana two meetings took place; one informal meeting at breakfast-time, between 7.00 and 8.00, and an official meeting at 10.00 to noon or something approximately at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, you are completely right in coming to that conclusion. If you allow me just to say I was not sure about the time of that first meeting. I expressed my doubts, even when I was giving my interview. But the second meeting did begin at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. Now, as to the official meeting, you told us that you didn't notice the presence of Mr. Krstic at the meeting, and you explained that if he had taken the floor, you would have noticed him; is that correct? Is it also correct that you learnt of the participation of Mr. Krstic to that meeting from the recordings you were able to see later on? Is that Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 148 to 153. correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, both your conclusions are completely correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Then basically, what you know of the participation of Mr. Krstic in that meeting is what you learnt later on from the recordings, so it's exactly what anybody could know looking at the recordings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I agree that you are completely right in noting this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: May I ask you if you have any additional information from other sources of the participation of Mr. Krstic to that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, I have never been shown, nor have I seen at any stage anything related to Mr. Krstic and his conduct at that meeting. Any additional information I had about the movements of Mr. Krstic after that meeting indicate that he continued to accompany the troops in the performance of their assignments. I cannot claim that it is correct information, but that is the information I had after the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Deronjic, may I come to the meeting -- to the informal meeting that took place in the morning. That meeting, you said, was convened by Mr. Mladic in order to prepare the official meeting. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Besides Mr. Mladic and yourself, you said that Mr. Simic, Mr. Vasic, and several others participated in that informal meeting. Can you be more precise as to the several others? How many, approximately, and could you identify anyone among them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, let me be precise. I remember Mr. Davidovic; he was president of the Executive Board of Bratunac municipality, and I noticed him at that meeting. And I said in my interview, if I'm not mistaken, that there may have been other people present. I did not identify the others. Most of the military commanders who were present in Bratunac on the ground on the 11th and the 12th are complete strangers to me. Maybe some of them attended that meeting, but I did not notice or identify them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Can you be more precise in answering my question when I put to you the question as to approximately how many people were in that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, I am certain about five people: Mr. Mladic, Mr. Simic, Mr. Vasic, Mr. Davidovic, and myself. About these I am certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So you cannot say how many people were in the room at the moment. Approximately, I mean. Were there 20, 30, 10? What was the size of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I cannot say with any certainty. I cannot give you a precise figure. I'm certain there were other people present. It was not an official, formal meeting, the kind that has an agenda. It was a more informal meeting. Waiters came and went, bringing refreshments, there might have been security men. Mladic was there at one point. But out of the relevant people, I really did not remark upon any of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask you whether you noticed Mr. Krstic among the participants or not.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, I met Mr. Krstic in one of the previous days, and I can claim that he was not at that meeting. I assert that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. That's what I wanted to know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I do have a couple of areas that I would like to follow up on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: First I would like to draw your attention to the military action itself of Western Slavonia. I believe you testified that the action itself occurred in Croatia on the 1st of May. Was that in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, if my memory serves me right, that operation took place in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And your understanding of that operation was that the fleeing column of Serbs included men, women, children, elderly, even livestock?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. I never said that I knew for certain whether it included livestock or not. I suppose that was impossible to know. What I said was that the reference of the president to those events was clear to me in the sense that there was one general shared opinion about the events in Slavonia, meaning that the troops and the civilians were fleeing together and were under attack by the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In the time between the 1st of May, 1995 and the 8th or 9th of July of 1995, did you hear President Karadzic talk about Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I first heard from President Karadzic just before the events in Western Slavonia. It was the topic at one of the meetings or informal gatherings that discussed these events in the light of one initiative, and that was the initiative of President Milosevic for the highway that crosses that province to be deblocked to enable communication, including by the army. President Karadzic expressed his opinion on that occasion, and I heard him saying that by acting in that way, President Milosevic actually enabled the offensive of Croatian forces against that area. And in his view, as he said, it was tantamount to handing over Western Slavonia into the hands of the Croatian army. That was the first thing I heard about the events in Western Slavonia. And then in the wake of the events in Western Slavonia, there was a meeting - I don't remember exactly where and when - where again these events were discussed and President Karadzic was furious about these events, and his fury derived mainly from the fact that his worst suspicions came true and that many Serbs fell victim, including a great number of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'd like to next direct your attention to a question that was asked by a member of the Bench with respect to the relationship of the military and civilian aspects of the government and the Republika Srpska. During the time period of January to May of 1995, did you know a General Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: In which period? Could you say again.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In 1995, leading up to May of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I did know General Zivanovic. He was the commander of the Drina Corps before being replaced by Mr. Krstic. He was also, I believe, the first commander in that area covered by the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, in fact, you were concerned about General Zivanovic, as you believed him to be incompetent.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. I was very unhappy with the conduct of Mr. Zivanovic in the area that was of particular interest to me, and that is the area covered by the Bratunac Brigade. I will only say that up to that period which we are discussing, in the area of the Bratunac Brigade, due to the well-known events around Srebrenica, there already had been around 500 casualties, including civilian victims. For all these things, I thought General Zivanovic was responsible because he was busy doing all sorts of other things rather than dealing with his primary responsibilities and duties. And just a few more words, if you allow me. I insisted --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Actually, I'd like to direct your attention to your concerns with respect to Mr. Zivanovic and whether you -- you expressed those concerns to President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, on more than one occasion I expressed my concern to President Karadzic, and in several informal and formal meetings of the personnel committee, I insisted that General Zivanovic be replaced, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And in fact, in May -- you believe it was May of 1995, President Karadzic pulled you aside after a meeting to tell you that your wish had been granted.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I said it could have been May, but I really cannot give you the exact date. He took me aside after a meeting and said that after several discussions with General Mladic, he had agreed with him that General Zivanovic would be replaced after all.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And in that same meeting where you were advised that General Zivanovic would be replaced, did President Karadzic advise you of any other information?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That, too, is correct. President Karadzic told me then for the first time that some kind of military operation will take place in the safe area; that means Srebrenica. That's all he said. And he added that I should be discreet about it and not talk about it much, and if I considered that any preparations were necessary, I should make them because we should be ready for this action.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'd next like to just clarify some of what you've said with respect to your relationship with the military. You were not in the military chain of information, were you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That is completely correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And your role was that of a political leader in the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That too is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yet you were able to communicate with President Karadzic with respect to military matters that he could then handle.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'd now like to direct your attention to your meeting in Pale on either the 8th or 9th of July. And first I want to ask you: Is there a way that -- or how is it that you're able to give a date to that particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: How was I able to give it or --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes. Is there a relationship between the time of your meeting and any other event that you can put those together with?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I understand your question now. There is another event with which I associated this date. I am allowing for the possibility that I'm mistaken about whether it is 8th or 9th, and let me tell you now it's also possible that it could have been the 7th or the 10th. There is, as I said, another event that helped me recollect this; namely, the fact that Mr. Borovcanin arrived the next day in Bratunac and I remember that this caused me to go to Pale. In any case, the lapse between two -- these two events cannot be more than two days.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I want to just clarify. Part of the reason that you went to Pale was your concern about bringing Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether this is an interpretation thing, but it was not about concern. There was concern about the troops that were involved in the operation around Srebrenica, and I wanted a well-trained unit to come to Srebrenica, and regardless of what kind of military operation it was, I wanted them to be involved. I had no further information about the military details of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And again, although you were a political leader, you were able to take those concerns about the military operation to President Karadzic for action.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That is true. I was able at any moment to convey to him my opinion, even about military matters, without going into how the president would or would not act upon it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And in this case, this is another example of where your concern resulted in a military action.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: How my concern led to a military action? It resulted in the arrival of Mr. Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And now I'd like to focus specifically on the sequence of your conversation with President Karadzic on the 8th or 9th of July. And specifically, I would like you to focus on Mr. Karadzic's words, where -- where we look. The first topic of discussion was the issue of the purpose of the military action on Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And the next area, then, was with respect to the military enforcement or reinforcement that needed to be brought in if that action was to be successful.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And then-President Karadzic asked you about what you - and I believe you said that was meant in the plural sense - intended to do with the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: He used the word "population"; I assume he meant civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And your response to that was that it was impossible for you to predict.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: What was his -- what were his direct words in response to that, as best you can recall them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, I have already repeated those words. He said, "All those down there, you need to kill them." "Whatever you get hold of," he added.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And then he talked about the principle of Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That is true too.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention now to the 12th of July. And just one question about the conversation -- the informal conversation that you had with General Mladic. You testified that he made vulgar comments with respect to President Karadzic and yourself.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did he do anything after that that you perceived as an apology for those comments?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did he send you breakfast after that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I did comment on the fact that in the office someone brought me or offered breakfast, and I inferred that it must have come from him. I apologise if I misunderstood. Now, if that is a gesture of apology, then it is true that he did in a sense apologise, if he was behind it, if he had sent the breakfast.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And now, although you've discussed at length some of the aspects of the meeting at the Hotel Fontana, I would like to talk about a particular area that President Karadzic wanted you to cover in that meeting, and that has to do with the men who may have been detained at Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did have instructions about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In fact, he asked you whether there were any men in this group detained at Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't quite put it like that. He said roughly - I'm not quoting him - but that there was a possibility that some people who may have committed war crimes could be hidden among those people there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... men.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And he directed you to insist that those people must be left behind.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That is true. I will tell you exactly what he said, that "If our civilian and military intelligence services have information about any of those men who may be hiding there or be among that group, then that they should be kept and that pursuant to the conventions governing war we were entitled to that and that I should say that publicly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: With respect to the overall meeting at -- at Hotel Fontana, you've described that as a farce. Would -- I want to make sure that we're characterising that correctly.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I have repeated that several times. That is my conviction.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And in fact, there were no options for the people who were detained there at Potocari, other than to be -- to leave.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That conclusion is your conclusion. I described the circumstances under which all that happened. I said that I presented three variants which I believe did not correspond to reality.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: You've previously -- or do you recall previously saying that the basic reason -- there was actually no true intention for them to stay but the whole thing was done for propaganda purposes, while the actual intent was to get them to leave the area and to clear the area of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I remember every sentence, and that is correct, and I said that that was my conclusion and my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: With respect to the meeting -- or the arrival of Colonel Beara on the night of the 13th of July, you've previously testified that he came in and said that he had established contact with those captives and that they should be killed.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand. Which contact are you referring to? Because he didn't tell me anything about having made contact with the captives but that he had come with instructions regarding those captives.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: For the record purposes, I'm referring to the Nikolic sentencing hearing, page 1548.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Do you recall testifying in that hearing?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And you've testified -- I believe you've advised this Chamber that your testimony there is correct.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: It is truthful and correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: So if you testified in that hearing - and I'm quoting you - that "He had established contact. He came in and said --" and I'm paraphrasing that section, but this is direct -- "that he had established contact with those captives and that they should be killed."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I may have said that. I do not consider that to be a relevant fact at all, whether he had had contact with them or not. I don't see how he could have had contact with them but that he had been assigned to take care of those people, that was obvious.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Let's go directly to the relevant portion of that. You would agree that he came in and said that they should be killed.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That is absolutely true.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And you were surprised that he was speaking so openly about such a sensitive topic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said that too.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In fact, you were so concerned about the topic that you wanted to get your friend, Mr. Simic, out of that room and away from that discussion.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That is also true. I said that too.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bibles. It's now 2.25, and I think that before going to the Defence, to give the floor to the Defence to ask questions of our witness, it might be convenient to have a short break now, say for 20 minutes. At quarter to 3.00 we will resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. Would the Defence wish to put questions to the witness? Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for giving me the floor. The Defence will have several questions for Mr. Deronjic, taking into consideration the time allotted to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deronjic, good afternoon. My name is Nenad Petrusic, and I represent General Krstic in this case.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The overall impression that the Defence is able to gain on the basis of your testimony today, and also knowing that since 1987 -- or rather, 1988, up until today, 2003, you had talks and interviews on a number of occasions with the Prosecutor, the overall impression is that you are extremely -- an extremely well-informed man regarding events in that area and the particular period I'm interested in, that is 1995, and the events in Srebrenica before its fall and after its fall in 1995. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Sir, you said 1988, but I assume you meant 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for your correction. In any event, I'm talking of the period from 1998 to the present.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That is true. I did have contacts with representatives of the OTP of this honoured Tribunal. And as I have informed the Prosecution, I was familiar with the events in Srebrenica. I didn't leave out any single detail. I think that I covered all my own activities and all my knowledge. To what extent that is -- that means that I'm extremely well informed, I don't know. There are things that I don't know in every detail, but I did convey all I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: For all those meetings, you prepared yourself, you spoke to people, you refreshed your memory about all the events of the period. Would that be a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: To a high degree, your statement is true. I would just say that I did refresh my memory in various stages of those interviews, but I would say that I had very little, if any, direct contact with the participants in those events. I knew I would have occasion to state what I knew, and I didn't wish in any way to involve others in what was happening here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Regarding your knowledge about the activities of General Krstic in that period, you were responding -- you have already answered questions by Their Honours, the Judges of this Chamber. I would like to know whether later on, through any investigations - if one can call them that - on your own, did you learn anything indirectly or did you gain any hearsay evidence about the participation of General Krstic in the crimes, to use a legal term, that occurred following the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, during the years following those events, to the extent it was possible, I did collect quite a bit of information about those events. I never came across any fact relating to General Krstic's involvement in what you correctly described as a crime that occurred following the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, let me now briefly turn to another topic, and that is the meeting at the Fontana Hotel on the 12th of July, 1995, starting at 1000 hours. You went to that meeting with instructions from the then-President Karadzic, which you had received in the evening by telephone, the previous evening, to convey one of three possible options: The first was for the civilian population to stay; the second, for it to leave; and thirdly, to go to third countries. The order of these options is not important for my question. My question is: Was as a consequence of that meeting the implementation of one of these three options? In other words, were the civilians from Potocari transported, deported, forcibly transferred, whichever legal term we will use will be determined by this Chamber but my question is: Was one of these three options observed and implemented?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, one of these three options was implemented, as you have described them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, with the permission of the Chamber and on condition the Prosecution has no objection, I should like to ask you a question, as in your interviews and in your testimony in the Nikolic case, and also today you presented quite a number of your own conclusions. I would like to ask you: What is your impression? Why did General Krstic not speak at that meeting, so that you never even noticed him there?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honours. I believe that Mr. Deronjic has testified that he didn't know General Krstic, except for one time, and that is strong speculation on his part in answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Counsel, I'm wondering whether the witness can really contribute more to the question on which he has been asked so many questions by the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will abide by your suggestion, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, on the 13th in the evening, Colonel Beara arrived with clear instructions from the top that those people should be killed. That is what you stated. That is not in dispute, is it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the transcript of the hearing in the Nikolic case, in which you testified, on page 1563, in answer to a question from the Prosecution whether Beara said anything to you which would indicate that he was the man that Karadzic had referred to, your answer was as follows: "I was not in a position to make that conclusion, or, rather, I was not able to establish a direct link, because President Karadzic's instruction were that the prisoners should be sent in the direction of Zvornik or Bijeljina, as I understood him. He started saying that the prisoners would be killed here. To be quite sure, at one point in time, he said, 'I have orders from the top.' I don't know who he meant. He didn't mention any names, but I think that the instruction could have come either from the Main Staff or from Mr. Karadzic." Is that correct, Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That is right, Mr. Petrusic. That is what I stated, and that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the same transcript, Mr. Deronjic, page 1569, in response to the Prosecutor's question, you answer: "If Karadzic had conveyed this order to Beara, then those intentions are quite clear to me, because he referred to the killing of those people. He had no instructions whatsoever that would go to show that Karadzic" - that's what you said - "no instructions whatsoever that would go to show that Karadzic gave such an order to Beara." Is this correct, Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, I would now like to go back to that meeting of the 8th or the 9th of July at Pale that you had with the then-President Karadzic, where he told you what he told you about the application of the principles of Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may ask the usher to prepare the exhibit from the case of Prosecutor against General Krstic, 432 from the trial stage -- from the pre-trial stage, that is, and to put it on the ELMO and give Mr. Deronjic the B/C/S version of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, you will receive the Serbian text of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Excuse me, could we ask for the exhibit number, please, so that we can identify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is Exhibit OTP 432. That is an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Yes. We see the exhibit now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if you allow me, I will continue with my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, in the last paragraph of this order, it says: "In accordance with the order of the president of Republika Srpska, an order has been issued to all combat units involved in combat operations around Srebrenica to provide maximum protection and safety to all UNPROFOR members and the civilian Muslim population. Order your subordinated units to refrain from destroying civilian targets unless they are forced to do so due to strong enemy resistance. Forbid the torching of residential buildings and treat the civilian population and prisoners of war in conformity with the Geneva Conventions of the 12th of August, 1949." Mr. Deronjic, this order that relays the order of President Karadzic, was issued at 2350 hours on the 9th of July, 1995. Bearing in mind this last paragraph, does it mean that -- in fact, can we infer that at this time President Karadzic gave up on the principles of Western Slavonia, as you understood them, in the morning hours of that same day, be it the 8th or the 9th of July?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic, I suppose that that inference can be made and that we can understand that events have taken a different course and the president issued orders accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence has concluded its examination of Mr. Deronjic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I would like to thank the counsel of the Defence, and I believe that we can now excuse the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would like to raise an issue with respect to that last line of questioning. And specifically -- obviously there are concerns about this witness answering questions as to President Karadzic's frame of mind with respect to a document that he's just been shown and has apparently no other knowledge of. Your Honours, we believe that that whole answer, frankly, should be stricken from the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, I would like to reserve our ruling on that. I will consult the Bench --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I take it, however, that you don't have comments about the physical state of that particular document as a -- an exhibit previously admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Sorry. I'll just answer that question. The document was previously admitted at trial, so of course the Prosecution has no objection to the document itself. The objection, of course, relates to the fact that this witness is in no position to refer to the state of the mind of an authorship of a document which he's never seen before on the basis of something shown to him for the first time today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will return to that topic after the break. We would now -- we would now call our next -- the next witness, who is Mr. Dragan -- First, let me thank you and excuse you from further proceedings. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Mr. President -- Mr. President, excuse me. If I may just -- if I may just address the Bench for one moment in between the witnesses. I'll wait until the witness leaves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Farrell.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to inform you that Ms. Bibles was here for the purpose of the questions of Mr. Deronjic and wanted to seek your leave that Ms. Bibles could leave and once again ask -- inform you that Mr. McCloskey is with the Prosecution, as he was involved with the next two witnesses, and ask your leave that he be permitted to sit at the table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. And I would like to thank Ms. Bibles for her contribution to our work, and wish her a pleasant afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Okay. We'll now call the next witness, who is Mr. Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Could I have, please, the attention of the counsel. Before the next witness comes. I have consulted my colleagues on the Bench, and we do not believe that we should strike out of record the question asked by the counsel for the Defence regarding that particular exhibit. Having said so, I would like to assure both parties that the Judges, as they always do, very carefully consider what kind of weight to attach both to the transcript itself and to the question asked by the Defence about that. So this -- the exchange between the counsel and Mr. Deronjic will not be struck off the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: We will now swear in the new witness, Mr. Obrenovic. Mr. Obrenovic, can you hear me? Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: You can -- before we ask you to read the solemn declaration, I understand that you have a lawyer representing you in the courtroom. And I would ask Mr. Dusan Slijepcevic to identify himself. You can hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. SLIJEPCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Slijepcevic, let me again emphasise, in accordance with our usual practice, that you may make interventions concerning your client's rights but not in relation to the factual basis of his testimony. And I would now ask Mr. Obrenovic, the witness, to please read the solemn declaration given you by the usher. Please read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. You may now be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, you will now be asked questions by the Defence, and after that you may be asked questions by the Prosecution. And I would invite the counsel for the Defence, please, to proceed. And I see Mr. Sepenuk is now standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sepenuk. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Obrenovic. I'm Norman Sepenuk, and along with my colleague, Nenad Petrusic, we represent General Krstic. I know that you recently testified in the case involving Colonel Blagojevic and Major Jokic. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You testified for a number of days in October, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, if all of the questions asked you at that trial were now asked of you again here, would your answer be the same?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's all I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I thank you, Counsel. I presume that the prior testimony will be regarded as part of our record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: And you do not wish to conduct any further examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. All of the testimony is -- has now been admitted into evidence. Mr. Farrell is urging the relevance of certain of the evidence. We are urging the relevance of other evidence. And I think it will become clear during the argument -- the specifics of our argument with respect to each item of testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Sepenuk. So I will now turn to the Prosecution. I understand that from your written submissions that you do not wish to conduct a cross-examination. Am I right on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So I believe that Mr. Obrenovic can now be -- unless my colleagues would like to ask questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Just if I can just clarify one matter. My understanding of the order originally was that the Defence would tender the witness for one purpose and the Prosecution would then tender him for another. In light of the fact that Mr. Sepenuk so kindly took care of all of it at one time and asked him if all his testimony was correct and if he adopted all of it, I don't see any need to proceed any further. And I thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So the parts in which you were interested are already now part of the record; and therefore, there's no need for further proceedings on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That's correct. And I just ask that they be admitted under Rule 89(F), pursuant to the Milosevic decision. I have copies of the complete transcripts that the Prosecution wishes to rely on, which I can tender with the registrar at any point in time for Mr. Obrenovic, so they'll be officially part of this record. They're the transcripts that we referred to in our motion for additional evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Is there any --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Just one thing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: We would like to do the same thing. Unfortunately, when we submitted our motion, our Rule 115 motion, we had an unofficial part of the transcript. And we'd like, with Your Honour's permission, to just submit the official transcript to the registrar at the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: But we are talking about exactly the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I see no problem with that. Is there any problem with excusing Mr. Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Obrenovic, thank you very much for your help, and you are now excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. You are free to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: You are, I take it, Mr. Momir Nikolic? Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you, Your Honours. I am Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that your counsel is present. May I ask Mr. Stefan Kirsch, please, to identify himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Excellency. Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Stefan Kirsch, I'm co-counsel for Mr. Nikolic, and together with me is Ms. Vesna Anic, my interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. And thank you for coming. Mr. Kirsch, you know that our usual practice is that you may make interventions concerning your client's rights but not in relation to the factual basis of his testimony. Mr. Nikolic, may I ask you now to please read the solemn declaration given to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. You may now be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Now, as we know, Mr. Momir Nikolic is appearing here as a witness in the rebuttal for the Prosecution. And I will now invite the Prosecution to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, and good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, Counsel, General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, do you recall testifying for several days in the trial of Mr. Blagojevic and Mr. Jokic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor, I remember testifying for eight days in one of these courtrooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you also remember at your sentencing hearing making clarifications on brief portions of that testimony at the trial?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that hearing. I mentioned my testimony, and at that hearing, among other things, I clarified to the Trial Chamber two issues, which I considered needed clarification. Of course, I can mention the two matters, if that is of interest to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It shouldn't be in detail at this stage; however, it may be. And I just have another question or two for you: If you were asked fundamentally the same questions that you were asked at trial, would your answers here today be -- be the same? And of course, taking into account the clarification that you'd made at your sentencing hearing.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In principle, yes, Mr. Prosecutor. The questions that I answered in the course of my testimony and the additional points of clarification would be my answer or the -- my complete answer to the two questions put to me. And, of course, on that occasion - and I wish to say that again now - that in order to clarify one of those matters, I offered documents to the Trial Chamber, a group of documents, which I still have in my possession and which I am offering now, which may serve to corroborate my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So I take it that the testimony -- trial testimony of Mr. Nikolic has been adopted for the purposes of the record before this Chamber. I take it that you have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Turning to the counsel for the Defence. It is my understanding, from your written submissions, that you do not wish to conduct an examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I just have one comment, though. Mr. Nikolic is, at the end of his testimony, mentioning that he has a number of documents that he'd like to submit but which apparently have not been submitted. I wasn't quite clear about that. I wonder if the Prosecutor might be able to enlighten us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Farrell, I'm not quite sure that this -- we should go into this question, but if you would like very briefly to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: The Prosecution position is I can indicate to the Court what this matter relates to, but in the Prosecution's position it is not relevant to the issues to which we are admitting his testimony or for which he is testifying today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's good enough for me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. So in the circumstances, I would like simply to thank Mr. Nikolic for his testimony. You may now leave the witness stand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I would like to consult the interpreters on our further proceedings. If the interpreters are tired, we would now have a break. If they are not tired, we would continue with the arguments -- oral arguments on the weight and -- of the evidence admitted by both parties. And so I am in the hands of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the interpreters could do with a short break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Sorry. I did not hear the last answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the interpreters would need a short break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So it will be. We will meet at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. Do I understand that the counsel for the Defence would like to make a motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: It has to do with the testimony of the Prosecution's military expert, Mr. Butler. And just by way of very brief background, the Prosecutor's Office had filed, very recently -- on November 18th, it filed a motion under Rule 68 to admit evidence of Mr. Butler, since Mr. Butler has again testified -- has testified recently in the Blagojevic and Jokic trials on this question of what does the meaning "up there," what is the meaning of the expression "up there"? Does it mean the battle area, or does it mean the around Branjevo Farm and Pilica Dom where the executions took place. And as Your Honours know, Mr. Obrenovic has now stated that "up there" meant the combat zone, where the combat was going on with the Bosnian Muslim column. And the lateness of arrival meant the troops from the Bratunac Brigade arrived there late, not at the execution site. Mr. Butler now agrees that that is a reasonable conclusion from the evidence. Now, I think it's fair to say that the Prosecution is not conceding the entire point. They're still going to claim, I believe that, General Krstic did send troops from the Bratunac Brigade to aid in the execution. We very vigorously contest that. But at least on this one aspect of the case, I think it's fair to say that the Prosecution now agrees that what Mr. Blagojevic testified to was a reasonable inference from the record and Mr. Butler agrees with that. So for that purpose, Your Honour, we're moving the introduction of Mr. Butler's testimony under Rule 115. With the Court's permission, we'd like to do the same thing either on Wednesday or Thursday - it will take a minute or so - simply ask Mr. Butler the same questions we asked Mr. Obrenovic and Mr. Nikolic, and I take it that this is a procedure at least that the Prosecution agrees with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sepenuk. We have heard your oral motion for admission into our case of the testimony of Mr. Butler from the Blagojevic -- Prosecutor against Blagojevic case. And I now turn to Mr. Farrell to confirm that in fact you are agreeable to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. President, Mr. Sepenuk has spoken to me about this. We have discussed it. My understanding is that the two annexes, Annex A and B, that were filed as the additional evidence on November 18th, that we have no objection to those two annexes being presented as his testimony from the Blagojevic case and that he will come to confirm them in a similar fashion as we've seen today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Farrell. So speaking on behalf of the Chamber, we grant this motion. And I would like you, Mr. Sepenuk, at the very beginning of our hearings on the merits on Wednesday morning to introduce this testimony as accepted into our record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Now, we are now turning to the last stage of our deliberations today, namely the oral arguments. And we will invite the counsel for both parties to present their oral arguments on the weight and on the credibility of the admitted evidence and of the rebuttal material. Now, first, I will give the floor to the counsel for the Defence and then to the counsel for the Prosecution. I remind the parties that each of them has 30 minutes of argument each. And counsel of the Defence, I would like to draw your attention to the following: If we -- you wish to reserve any portion of the 30 minutes allotted to you for a reply, please plan it accordingly and let me know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I'd like to reserve 10 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: By the way -- excuse me, Your Honour. I had a podium here. I don't know where -- oh, I think the Prosecution thought they were going to speak first, so they took my podium. I don't know -- it's not totally necessary for me to have it, but if it's available --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I -- I see. So no more war crimes here of plunder of podiums. Okay, Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Twenty minutes now and then the Prosecution and then you have ten more minutes. It's ten past 4.00, so you can go until 4.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'd like to start, Your Honours, with the Deronjic testimony. The Trial Chamber, in 360 of its opinion, stated that it was apparent that the Prosecution built its case on the theory that the plan to execute the Bosnian Muslim men of Srebrenica was devised in the evening hours of 11 July and the early morning hours of 12 July 1995. And I respectfully suggest that nothing that has taken place here today should alter that finding of the Trial Chamber. Genocide is too important and serious a matter to be left to the kind of testimony that the government is relying on vis-a-vis Mr. Deronjic. A single conversation on July 8th or 9th with President Karadzic, according to Mr. Deronjic, about "all of them must be killed," the government is trying to translate and convert into a genocidal plan to kill the Bosnian Muslims as a group. That simply should not be. That was a single conversation. It was tentative. It was optional. It depended upon what happened, if indeed there was going to be a takeover of Srebrenica, and a comparison was made to Western Slavonia. I'm not an expert on the Western Slavonian situation, but as I understand it, it had to do with the fleeing of civilians and troops together, fleeing from Western Slavonia, and under those circumstances it was thought legitimate. Indeed, it is not legitimate, but it was thought legitimate that perhaps there could be shelling and killing. But it was a single conversation, and the fact of the matter is nothing ever happened, because the very next day, on July 9th, 1995, we have this letter from General Tolimir, which specifically refers to the president of the Republika Srpska, President Karadzic, giving orders to refrain from destroying civilian targets, ban the torching of residential buildings, treat the civilian population and war prisoners in accordance with the Geneva Conventions of 12 August 1949. So it's obvious, as Mr. Deronjic said, the government didn't like his answer, so they objected to it, but that he did indeed, the next day, change his mind. And there was nothing to controvert what this letter reveals: It was a single conversation, it was tentative, it was optional. And it should really be given little if any weight, I respectfully suggest, by Your Honours. After that we get to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: -- and of course, President Karadzic gives -- excuse me -- gives three options to Mr. Deronjic to let -- let the people go or they can stay, or they can go to a third country if they like. Now, that may indeed have been a smoke screen. Initially, when I saw the -- the testimony from Mr. Deronjic many, many months ago, which we claim was not turned over to us, in violation of Rule 68 - and incidentally, Your Honour did turn down our request under Rule 68 -- under Rule 115 to admit that evidence - it was our belief that this was not a smoke screen, that this was genuine, and we had already told Your Honours we were not going to proceed with our forcible transfer argument because we respect the Delalic appeal rationale and the other appellant Chamber holding that just because you disagree with the Trial Chamber and just because there's a bunch of other evidence to the contrary, you know, that's -- that's it. And we say that with reluctance, because we did feel there was a large body of evidence supporting a voluntary transfer. We're not making that argument, and we're particularly not making that argument now in view the fact that Mr. Deronjic has now gone back on his earlier testimony. He now says it was a smoke screen. And I -- I will accept that. It was a smoke screen because the prisoners were going to be transferred. It was obvious that General Mladic particularly had created a situation where the -- where the civilians had to go. And that was what the smoke screen was all about. It wasn't a smoke screen on killings. There's no suggestion in this record that it was a smoke screen to cover up killings, because as the July 9th letter states, there were to be no killings. The killing plan, if we can call it that, wasn't devised, as the Trial Chamber said, until the night of the July 11th or the latest, July 12th, when it was discovered that there were men being separated from the group at Potocari and then, of course, the Bosnian Muslim column of men escaping toward Tuzla. And again, the facts speak for themselves. The civilians were never harmed. The civilians were transported in safety, incidentally under orders from General Krstic, not a hair on their head should be harmed. And of course, it goes without saying that General Krstic never had any part in these proceedings. He was an invisible person. Mr. Deronjic didn't even remember that he was at the meeting until he saw that -- he saw the tape. Then we get to the night of July 13th -- to the day -- to July 13th, and we have the visit from Mr. Beara. Now, again, Mr. Beara had to have come from General Mladic, not President Karadzic. And we've summarised all of our argument on that point in -- in what's already been presented to the Court in -- in our response to the Prosecution's submission. I don't think I should take the time to read it, but we've already said, and Mr. Petrusic established with Mr. Deronjic, that he didn't have any information which would demonstrate that Karadzic gave the orders to Mr. Beara, and it's obvious to us that Colonel Beara was on a mission of the Main Staff, and it was unrelated to the conversation between Deronjic and Karadzic on 8 or 9 July. The orders came -- the top, meaning they came from the top; that means General Mladic, not President Karadzic. Because if President Karadzic had made this order to Beara, he would have just followed it. He would have followed it. As it was, Deronjic said, "No, no, you cannot kill these prisoners in Bratunac," and then Beara folded up his tent and went away. More indication - I think conclusive indication - that it was General Mladic and not President Karadzic who were giving the orders. I'd like to turn to the Obrenovic testimony that was admitted under Rule 115. I've already given a preview of it. This was -- this was one of the most important parts of our case. We firmly believe that General Krstic never gave any orders for members of the Bratunac Brigade to go to Branjevo Farm or Pilica Dom to assist in those executions. We feel very strongly about that, and we feel that the government's evidence has now fallen with Obrenovic's testimony and Butler's testimony. This is a major subject, and I want to be careful about my time. Mr. Petrusic, I think, is going to be spending a very large amount of time on this point, because this is the only direct evidence in the case which shows General Krstic's knowledge of a killing plan. I underline that. The only direct evidence in this case that shows General Krstic's direct knowledge of a killing plan is that 15 July 1995 conversation he had with Colonel Beara. And we're saying he said, to get Beara off his back, forgive my language, "Fuck it, I'll see what I can do." The fact of the matter is he never did anything. And the Obrenovic testimony and the Butler testimony is going to establish just that. Exhibits 1, 2, and 3, they show essentially that the capture -- I'm talking about tabs 1, 2, and 3, Your Honours. It shows that the capture and the execution was a Main Staff MUP operation. It says, "We are not --" Mr. Vasic says in one of the letters, "We're not getting any help from the VRS. We're doing this alone. We're doing the annihilation of the men and we're doing the capturing by ourselves. We're not getting any help on this." Mind you, this is 13 July 1995 at a time when General Krstic, as the Trial Chamber recognised, was heavily involved in Zepa. He was there. He was appointed the commander of the Zepa operation the evening of July 11th. As Mr. Obrenovic said, in the testimony that has now been admitted, he called General Krstic on 15 July to tell him about the Bosnian Muslim column. General -- Mr. Obrenovic said - and it's in one of our submissions - "General Krstic didn't seem to know what was going on. He had no idea what was happening here." In any event, these Exhibits 1, 2, and 3 prove that, and we expect to argue that later next -- next week at the oral argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But that particular witness, I think that Your Honours, under the circumstances, are justified to giving his statement rather minimal weight. The point of his statement was to show particularly that members of the military police were subordinate to the Main Staff security organs, and many times acted without the knowledge of Drina Corps personnel, including upper level Drina Corps personnel and including even up to General Krstic. We believe that at the very least, with Mr. Obrenovic's testimony now, at the very least it's been established that it was discretionary for members of the security organs to -- whether or not to notify a particular Drina Corps commander as to what was happening. That instruction, I believe, should not be -- by the way, the one remaining evidentiary matter in this case is the -- is that instruction of 1994 from General Mladic. And I'm not sure the Court has ever ruled on its admissibility. But without General Radinovic, you've now excluded General Radinovic from testifying, without General Radinovic, that instruction would not be very meaningful. So without his testimony and without the instruction, I think the -- our position has been watered down, but at the very least it's -- it's established by the evidence that the -- it was discretionary on the part of the security forces whether or not to notify the Main Staff. And our submission is that on the -- on some -- certain very crucial aspects of the case, General Krstic was never notified. And we're going to discuss that in some detail next week. Thank you, Your Honour. And again, I -- I apologise for my omission before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now invite Mr. Farrell for his --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you. If I may, Your Honour, I'd like to introduce Mr. Moylan, who's a member of the appeals section and who has not had the opportunity to appear before you today but who will be making submissions on behalf of the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Moylan, I would welcome you here and invite you to make your presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOYLAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: You have until five minutes before 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOYLAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President and members of the Bench, I'd like to begin by just briefly outlining the submissions that I'm going to make. I'm going to divide the submissions into three parts essentially. The first portion, I'm going to deal with a number of outstanding issues very briefly and the Prosecution's position on those issues in anticipation for the final phase of argument. These are issues that will specifically relate to weight and credibility of certain pieces of evidence. Then I will address the remaining evidence, first dealing with Mr. Deronjic, and then turning to the other evidence of both the rebuttal evidence from the Prosecution and the additional evidence from the Defence. So if I may, starting with the areas that remain outstanding areas of dispute between the parties, the principal areas of dispute. The Prosecution position, beginning with the tab 5 evidence, has been stated before on the record. And I would just restate that briefly, that the Prosecution's position is that untested witness statements should not form part of the record for purposes of returning a verdict, a matter as serious as that, particularly when they have not been subjected to the procedural safeguards of Rule 92 bis. And the Prosecution obviously noted that the tab 5 witness was not in court and therefore was not able to be subjected to cross-examination and submits that his material should be given de minimis, if any, weight on that basis. Furthermore, the Prosecution would just briefly refer the Chamber to its submissions regarding the tab 5 witness. In the Prosecution response to Defence motion of support Rule 115, dated 15 August 2003, in which we set out further detailed submissions on the reliability and credibility of that witness. The second area that I'd like to address that remains of some contention is the evidence that the Defence has sought to rely on for Mr. Obrenovic regarding the interpretation of a particular intercept that the Trial Chamber referred to in its judgement. And specifically the intercept that I'm referring to is quoted at paragraph 401 of the judgement. And just very briefly on the subject matter, it concerns a conversation between the Drina Corps security chief and a member of the -- a member of the -- excuse me, the Drina Corps operations officer at the Drina Corps command. And it's regarding -- as it's utilised in the trial judgement, it concerns reporting to Krstic -- or an attempt to report to General Krstic regarding certain activities. The Prosecution position on that, very briefly, is that the -- Mr. Obrenovic's interpretation of the intercept, as he's provided recently in court, is a reasonable interpretation. The Prosecution accepts that, and that it could have been a factor -- it could have resulted in the Trial Chamber giving a portion of the intercept a different interpretation but that, in light of the trial judgement as a whole, that it would not have been a decisive factor in reaching the verdict on any -- any particular factual finding. And with that said, I will defer to my colleagues next week, who are going to elaborate on that issue at some greater length. The next issue that I'll briefly address is the rebuttal document, Annex 7 from the Prosecution, which the disputed issue concerns the authenticity of the signature of that document. It is a Drina Corps -- it appears to be a Drina Corps daily combat report to the Main Staff dated the 13th of July, in which the Drina Corps is reporting certain activities that are occurring in its zone of responsibility having to do, among other things, with the search of the terrain, to try to capture Muslim prisoners, and also related ambush activities. The Prosecution would first note Mr. Obrenovic's testimony in this regard, which it filed recently in its supplemental to the Prosecution motion regarding the admissibility of this document that I'm discussing, the Drina Corps daily combat report. This is Registry page number A5006. And briefly, Mr. Obrenovic provides what we submit is very substantial evidence to corroborate and give the document indicia of reliability, which should allow the Chamber to consider it with some weight. The first point that Mr. Obrenovic mentions in his testimony on this document, he's shown a copy of it in court and asked to comment on it, and he indicated that the background for these type of reports is that the constituent brigades of the Drina Corps would prepare information regarding what's happening in their zone of responsibility and they would then forward that to the Drina Corps, which would in turn prepare its own daily combat report and forward that to the Main Staff. Obrenovic further said that based on his knowledge of what was happening in the terrain at the time, where he was personally deployed, that the order -- or the combat report as it was formulated and he read it appeared to be an accurate reflection of what actually was happening to his understanding, which he was in a -- a very good position to know what was happening because he was deployed in the field at that time. And furthermore, he commented, based on his experience with General Krstic as a subordinate, that the signature on the document looked to him like General Krstic's signature. The Prosecution would also note an exhibit that was tendered during the trial. The exhibit number is 463, and it is an order which is acknowledged to have been signed by General Krstic and sent to its selected units subordinate to it regarding search activities. And the reason we bring this up, Your Honours, is because when you review - and I won't go into the details - but when you review the Prosecution Exhibit 463 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down a little for the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOYLAN
utterances.text: -- annex, what you'll see is that the -- what you'll see is that the subject matter concerned in each document is practically identical. In other words, there are search activities being conducted around Srebrenica involving forces of two particular units, and they're mentioned in both reports, so they concern overlapping subject matter. They're both issued on the 13th of July, and they would provide further indicia of reliability for the challenged document.
