The Prosecution just briefly notes that there has been no challenge raised by the Defence to Mr. Nikolic's testimony, and we would further note that as to both Mr. Nikolic and Mr. Obrenovic, the evidence that they provided on the propositions for which the Prosecution submitted their evidence is particularly compelling in light of the positions that they held during the operation. Mr. Nikolic, it will be remembered, is the Bratunac Brigade assistant commander for security and intelligence. He's provided information about the parallel chain of command which the Defence has raised as an issue, and he has in essence said as to the parallel chain of command that it didn't exist, to his knowledge. He was in direct command of the commanding officer, the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, and he furthermore stated that as to the issue of reporting, that while there could be in very limited circumstances sealed correspondence between the Bratunac Brigade security organ and its senior security organ in the Drina Corps, that this was an extremely rare occurrence, and to his knowledge, from approximately July to November of 1995, it never occurred. Furthermore, Mr. Nikolic has provided extremely compelling evidence regarding events on the 12th of July, outside of the Fontana meeting, which we've discussed earlier today. And in particular, Mr. Nikolic was providing security outside the meeting while General Krstic, General Mladic, Mr. Deronjic, and other members of the military and civilian leadership were inside meeting with the Muslim and the DutchBat authorities. As Mr. Nikolic is outside of that same meeting, outside the hotel, he has a conversation with two -- with two senior officers in the Drina Corps and subordinates of General Krstic who advise Mr. Nikolic of the plan to separate the men in Potocari and then carry out the executions of those men. Mr. Obrenovic has provided very similar information regarding his activities in the Zvornik Brigade a short time later. Mr. Obrenovic is the acting commander of the Zvornik Brigade, and again is in a -- a perfect position to know how the functioning of the security organs and the other issues that are raised by the Defence, such as the military police, how these areas would function. His testimony is as -- is very briefly summarised as follows: Mr. Obrenovic has said in the Nikolic trial, which has now been incorporated here, that on the 13th of July his security chief came to him as he was serving as acting commander of the Zvornik Brigade and advised him that he had -- that the security chief had been informed of a plan to execute the Muslim prisoners and that they would be transported to Zvornik to be executed. Mr. Obrenovic at that point responded that, "We can't undertake such an operation without the support of our -- first of all, our brigade commander, but also without reporting to the Drina Corps," which would be General Krstic and the Drina Corps command. And the response from the security chief is quite telling, because he said, "There's no need to report. The orders came from Mladic and our commander knows and everybody knows." So at that point in time, Mr. Obrenovic undertook to assist in the operation by providing support in various ways. There again, we would submit that as to the issue of the parallel chain of command, which the Defence has raised in a number of their pieces of evidence, including the tab 5 evidence and the reports, tabs 1 through 3, on all of that evidence we would submit that you should give great weight to the testimony of key players from the Zvornik Brigade and, in fact, the only security officer whose testimony is in these proceedings, Momir Nikolic, who have essentially said that the parallel chain of command was non-existent for purposes of the Srebrenica operation. Your Honour, the Defence has also raised in the tab 5 evidence the issue of the military police control. I won't go into that in any length because of the submissions that we've made as to the quality of that evidence, but I would simply refer the Chamber to our prior submissions, which it's -- it's in the Prosecution's further notice of rebuttal evidence. Here again, both Mr. Nikolic and, much more importantly, Mr. Obrenovic have provided very telling evidence as to the control of the military police units and have made it quite clear that the brigade commanders, or in this case Mr. Obrenovic as the acting commander, had the ability to control the military police and deploy them as they saw fit. And in fact, in the Zvornik Brigade area, when the security chief wanted to determine what to do about the prisoners and wanted to request assistance which would involve the military police, he didn't take them, he actually asked Obrenovic as the acting brigade commander if he could -- if Obrenovic would deploy those -- some of those units to him, and Obrenovic undertook to do that. So there again we would say that as things actually applied in the Srebrenica operation, it's quite clear from the evidence of both Mr. Obrenovic and Mr. Nikolic, who were in a very good position to know, that this -- that the military police were squarely under the brigade command. The next issue -- the next factual proposition which is raised in the Defence evidence is the activities of the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior -- the Ministry of the Interior forces. These forces, it will be remembered, are deployed along the central -- the road where a lot of the Muslim forces were captured as they were trying to flee the Srebrenica enclave. And Mr. Vasic should be noted at this time was the head of the municipal police for Zvornik. His reports, the Defence has put forward, as they've alluded to today, for the proposition that the MUP was carrying out operations and activities on their own but -- well, directly from Mladic and the VRS Main Staff but without the involvement or knowledge of the Drina Corps. And Your Honour, here again we would refer to a number of propositions in both the judgement, which very amply recounts the evidence at trial, and specifically noting in paragraphs 283 to 289 the Trial Chamber recited the evidence and reached the finding that while the Court wasn't able to find a command relationship between the MUP and the Drina Corps that certainly the evidence that the Court had before it convinced it that there was close cooperation and coordination between the MUP and Drina Corps units. And we would add to that the rebuttal evidence from Mr. Obrenovic in particular on this issue. Mr. Obrenovic has recounted a series of contacts that he had, beginning on the 12th of July, as the first prisoner started to be taken as they were fleeing and crossing the road, which -- the central road where the MUP was deployed. He's described a series of contacts that he had with the MUP throughout the entire subsequent operation. I won't go through that, in the interest of time, but I would again refer the Court to the Prosecution's further notice regarding its rebuttal evidence, filed on the 20th of October, 2003. With that said, Your Honours, I will now turn to the evidence of Mr. Deronjic, which the -- which the appellant's counsel has provided submissions on. The appellant is quite correct to say that Mr. Deronjic's evidence does not directly implicate General Krstic. It's -- it's quite clear that he had some very limited contact at the forward command post of the Drina Corps and then had another contact, though they didn't even exchange words, at the Fontana meeting. The nature of the Prosecution's theory as to this evidence, though, is of a different nature. In particular, the Prosecution has expressed the view in its submission of Mr. Deronjic's evidence that the evidence can be used as a lens, if you will, to view the subsequent conduct and activities and events that take place throughout the operation. And in that sense, they can be of assistance to the Chamber in looking at the events as they unfolded to see how they make sense. And in particular, the -- the Prosecution would submit that when the evidence is used in this way, what becomes more clear than it was before is that there was an overall strategic purpose, depending on how events unfolded in the Srebrenica enclave, and that the purpose was a purpose to commit genocide but there was not necessarily an operational plan that could be formulated at that early stage, because it was unknown, as you heard Mr. Deronjic tell us, it was unknown exactly what the responses would be of the civilians within the community. But the purpose included, as it -- as it clearly included from the factual record, a series of things which are quite telling, in light of the evidence. The military operations, according to the Trial Chamber, were designed to create a humanitarian crisis within the enclave. Furthermore, on the 10th and 11th and continuing to the 12th of July - this is actually before and then after the takeover of Srebrenica - there was indiscriminate shelling of the Muslim population in the enclave, including while the Muslim civilians were actually making the trip from the Srebrenica town to Potocari. There are indications in the trial record as to a lack of provision of adequate food, water, and medical assistance for refugees. It was not provided for in the plan. And furthermore, the -- the trial record is replete with evidence of a spreading wave of mistreatment and killings, and escalating throughout the operation. Of course, we know how the operation culminated, and it's quite ironic, in our submission, to have the appellant cite two pieces of isolated evidence, the document from General Tolimir, and then furthermore the statement of General Krstic not to harm a hair on the refugees' heads in light of the overall circumstances. And that -- that is the nature of this evidence, is that it -- it needs to be applied in the context of the overall events. I think it -- it would be of assistance to briefly set out some of the points that help to provide that context, in order to understand how the comments help to show a purpose that was applied consistently throughout the operation and was limited only by the kind of factors that Mr. Deronjic talked about, like the involvement of the UNPROFOR forces and the international media attention, which constrained the initial purpose that the Prosecution would submit existed and actually had to -- the operational plans had to be changed in order to suit the circumstances. First of all, starting with the initial circumstances of the position of President Karadzic. You've heard he was the Supreme Commander of the armed forces. That includes both the military and the MUP forces. In reference to the Western Slavonia principle, it's -- it's quite interesting that that principle was invoked in the sense that it involved the shelling of civilian -- a mixed civilian and military column of Serbs living in Western Slavonia. We see something quite like that, actually, in the town of Srebrenica being heavily shelled on the 10th and 11th of July, and then the Muslim column, which was largely comprised of civilians, making their way to Potocari and being shelled again rather indiscriminately. The further circumstances that I would briefly note as to the military takeover: General Krstic was a principal participant in the planning of Krivaja 1995 in terms of the military operations as they unfolded. That was why he was at the forward command post, as you heard Mr. Deronjic mention. And the Court found this, that he was principally involved in the planning. When President Karadzic issued the order to take the Srebrenica enclave, the order was issued specifically to General Krstic because of his close involvement in the operation, and all of this happened within a few days, literally two to three days, of the conversation that was being conducted between Mr. Deronjic and President Karadzic. The close time connection would reinforce the view that the comments as they were uttered at that time were at a time when the enclave was nearly ready to fall, and the Serbs were engaged in the shelling of the enclave at that stage and then the events unfolded from there. The further circumstances as to the operational planning in Bratunac, the -- the appellant has mentioned the Trial Chamber's findings that operational plans to forcibly transfer and -- to transfer, I'll say, and to carry out mass executions were formulated between the 11th and the 12th. That's actually quite consistent with the evidence from President -- from Mr. Deronjic regarding President Karadzic in the sense that, as I said before, at the stage that the comments were uttered there couldn't necessarily be an operational plan because there were too many variables and Mr. Deronjic in fact even referred to that when he replied to President Karadzic as to, "I can't speculate as to what will happen with the civilian population." Again, referring to some of the circumstances in Bratunac surrounding the Fontana meeting, I've already referred to Major Nikolic, who, on the morning of the 12th, at the time that we've heard of the meeting in today's evidence, the operational plan to separate and execute the men was clearly in existence at that point in time. And the Court also found that the operational plan to transfer the women and children and -- and the elderly and boys was also -- was also formed by that time. You heard Mr. Deronjic talk about - and it's developed in the trial judgement already - but the night before that, the 11th of July, which was the takeover of Srebrenica, General Mladic had issued an ultimatum that the Muslim population in Potocari could survive or disappear. The senior officials in Bratunac at the time of the Fontana meeting included such people as Generals Mladic and Krstic, various Main Staff officers, General Zivanovic, the Drina Corps commander at that moment in time, soon to be replaced in the Prosecution's case, theory, Mr. Deronjic, and then also senior MUP officials. The nature of the operation was clearly one that incorporated and involved a massive amount of resources and personnel, and so the tasks were being divided up among the VRS, the -- the different elements of the VRS, the Main Staff, the Drina Corps, the subordinate brigades, and the MUP as well, with Deronjic also playing some role in terms of the planning process. The Drina Corps subordinates of General Krstic, at the -- at the time are also noted in the trial judgement, but they include some of the persons that I've mentioned already; the security and intelligence officer for the Drina Corps who advised Major Nikolic of the plan to execute the prisoners. And I'll just briefly mention the implementation as it unfolded in the subsequent days. The Trial Chamber was able to find, based on the evidence that was before it, that as of the 13th of July, based on a succession of events, including a mass execution which occurred in the MUP area of responsibility, that General Krstic and the Drina Corps must have known by that point that the killing operation was unfolded. And furthermore, it's quite telling, in the Prosecution's submission, that Colonel Beara, who's been the subject of testimony today, also shares a linkage to General Krstic two days later, on the 15th of July, when they have an intercept which is accepted by the Trial Chamber as concerning mass executions. So Your Honour -- Your Honours, just briefly, the nature of the case is one that involves so many parts and so many pieces that Mr. Deronjic's evidence is not by any means sufficient on its own to link to General Krstic, and the Prosecution wouldn't submit that, but the overall inferences that develop when you review the trial judgement and the Prosecution's rebuttal evidence, we submit, establishes a compelling case that the operational plan to take Srebrenica and then to devise mass execution plan and forcible transfer plan, were actually being guided, if you will, by a larger strategic plan, which is established at least as of the time of the conversation that Karadzic has. And the last thing that I will say is the nature of the contact at the -- at the SDS office that Mr. Deronjic has with Colonel Beara on the night of the 13th bears some scrutiny. Mr. Deronjic himself talked about these events in fairly clear terms today, but the contact that he had with President Karadzic was only a few hours before Colonel Beara walked into his office, and the nature of their conversation was, "We have massive problems in Bratunac with the prisoners who are creating a security problem, and we need to do something about it," and that was the insistence that Mr. Deronjic spoke about when he talked to President Karadzic. And President Karadzic said, "Somebody will come and somebody will come with instructions and will take care of the prisoners." And within a few hours somebody did arrive, and in fact nobody else arrived, and the next day, when President Karadzic and Mr. Deronjic talked about it, the question was the interpretation of his comment that "These soldiers are fools." And Mr. Deronjic discussed the two options that occurred to him in terms of how to interpret that comment and provided what the Prosecution would submit is a reasonable interpretation of those words, that President Karadzic in a position to influence and effect, as the Supreme Commander of the armed forces, what would occur with the prisoners in the ensuing days took no steps to -- that is better known to stop that process. And to Mr. Deronjic sitting in the meeting, that's the conclusion that he was able to draw later reflecting on it. So the Prosecution submits that there is a strong inference that President Karadzic was the one who was ultimately responsible for Colonel Beara's arrival and that perhaps it operated through the VRS Main Staff. Your Honour, with that, I would be able to conclude. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. And I will now ask counsel for the Defence to take the remaining ten minutes that he has --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: -- to complete his oral argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'll be brief. I don't think I'll take the ten minutes. It's interesting that at this stage of the proceedings, after a trial, after the admission of additional evidence, the Prosecution still uses a term that was used by the Trial Chamber repeatedly, that General Krstic "must have known." And on page 31, I believe, or 30, 31, 32 of our brief, we set forth the comments of the Trial Chamber on their various factual findings. General Krstic must have known. He could only have known. He could only surmise. And it's the point we're trying to make and the point we expect to make in some detail next week is that under -- certainly under the Delalic appeal rationale, where a case is based upon, as the Trial Chamber said in this case, layer upon layer of circumstantial evidence and where you're seeking to infer intent, the Court must look at the only reasonable conclusion to be derived from the evidence. It must be the only reasonable conclusion. If there is a conclusion consistent with innocence, the Court should have adopted that conclusion. And nowhere is that more graphically illustrated by this -- the last point the Prosecutor made, with respect to the visit of Colonel Beara. We have already offered in our written submissions evidence to show that the order from the top did not come from President Karadzic; it came from General Mladic. That is certainly a reasonable conclusion in the evidence. But the Prosecutor, looking at it through its own - I say very respectfully - murky lens, the Prosecutor says that the Deronjic testimony provides a lens to look through in terms of gauging future events. It's a very distorted lens, it's a very murky lens, and I think that it should be given little, if any, weight by the Court. And then our general submission is that the Court should look at the -- should adopt, and indeed must adopt, the Delalic appeal rationale. And as we expect to get into much greater detail next week, the -- the inference that we're going to ask the Court to find is that certainly General Krstic did not have genocidal intent and General Krstic did not have the intent to murder or to exterminate. The forcible transfer issue is out of the case. I might as well say that now. Because of the Court's ruling on the Deronjic evidence and because of subsequent developments relating to Deronjic, we're not going to be arguing the forcible transfer portion of the case. But what we will be arguing is a lack of any joint criminal enterprise intent and a fortiori no criminal intent whatever on the part of General Krstic to commit genocide nor has the Prosecution shown beyond a reasonable doubt that General Krstic had the intent to commit -- had the intent to formulate a murder plan or to aid and assist the murder plan. Again, and I'll end this with: The only direct evidence in the case of his knowledge of a killing plan was the July 15th, 1995 conversation with Colonel Beara. And we think the evidence shows that he did not follow through on it, that troops from the Bratunac Brigade never came to assist in executions, that -- that General Krstic never had any kind of genocidal or any other intent to kill the Bosnian Muslim men, and he never aided and assisted that operation. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sepenuk, for your argument in response. With your comments, we have concluded our agenda for today. I would like to thank the counsel for the parties for their contributions. As you know, we will reconvene to hear the merits of the appeal at 9.30 a.m. on Wednesday, the 26th of November, and we will start with the 115 motion, which we have granted and which I hope will only take two or three minutes so we can proceed to the hearing on the merits. So again, thank you. And we will now rise.
